THE ROYAL JUBILEE. These fifty years Victoria The nation's pride has been; The noblest of illustrious line, Our well-beloved Queen! The good times in her gracious reign Will long remembered be; Then let us greet Victoria, Our noble Queen Victoria, With Royal Jubilee! Over her wide domain, Long may Victoria reign! Long may she reign! Empress and Queen Victoria! May God preserve Victoria, And bless her Jubilee! What nation can we find on earth So favoured and so blest; Our commerce spreads the wide world o'er, Our arts through east and west! Our good Quee,n reigns! her peaceful sway • Extends from sea to.sea; With pride we hail Victoria, CiMi Our noble Queen Victoria, And keep her Jubilee! Through many yelrs still may she rule (Ter stalwart sons and brave, Who nobly bear the British flag On distant land or wave ! . From lokal hearts, through all the land, Her people's prayer shall be: Defend, 0 Lord, Victoria, Our noble Queen Victoria, And bless her Jubilee! Hormg„ Author of " ifyntras and Songs."

"Indeed, it happened in less time than I take to tell it," said the lady, who was considered somewhat of a bore. "Oh, I haven't the least doubt of that," replied her patient and truthful listener. "Madame," he began, as he lifted his hat at the front door, "1 .am soliciting for home charities. We have hundreds of poor, ragged. and rude children like those at your gate, and our object is—" "Sir, those are any own children," and the front door was violently slammed to. Luttrell (says Moore) once told of an' Irishman who, having jumped into the water to save a man from drown- ing, upon receiving sixpence from the person as a reward for the service, looked first at the sixpence, then at him, ' and at last exclaimed, "By jabers, rm over-paid for the job." " The'great trouble with you, John, is," said a lady to her husband, who was suffering from the effects of the night before," you cannotaaye No.' Learn to say 'No,' John, and you will have fewer headaches. Can you let me have a little money this morning "No," said John, with apparent ease. Greville writes on one occasion—Moore told several stories which I don't recollect. And this amused us— Some Irish had emigrated to some West Indian colony; the negroes soon learnt their brogue, and when another shipload of Irish came soon after, the negroes, as they sailed in, said, " Ah, Paddy, how are you?" "What," said one of them, " y're become black already !" Morgan John O'Connell, nephew of the agitator, had (says Harrison) the ready wit of his country in a remarkable degree. We were walking by the Wei, one day when an Oxford graduate, a Mr. White, who had a taste for botany, plucked a flower ( Balsamum impatiens) from the river, remarking that "it was a very rare plant" "it is an out-of-the- W'ey, one, at any rate," was the reply. Party spirit in Dublin was at on,: time attended by continual duels. It was upon one of these occasions that Giffard, the editor of the Dublin Joternal, being called out, appeared on the ground with his spectacles en. This was objected to by his adversary's second, and he was desired to taka them off, which he did, exclaim- ing, "By my soul, this is too bad. I could not see to shoot my own father without them." A young fop, who has just begun to shave for a beard, stepped into a barber's shop, and after a grand swagger desired to be shaved. The barber went through the usual movements, and the sprig jumped up vzith a flourish, and exclaimed, "My foul fellow, what is the charge !" "Oh, no charge!" replied the barber. "No charge! How is that ?" "Why, I'm always thankful when I can get a soft calf skin to sharpen my razor on." A traveller in western lowa, noticing on the wall of the parlour of the hotel the legend, lei on parle Franeais, said to the proprietor: "Do you speak French?" " French ? No. United States is good 'nough for me." "Then why do you keep that legend on the wall? That means 'French is spoken here:" "Is that so ?" "Cer- tainly." "Well, I'm a half-breed from up the Missoury if a feller with a wart on his nose didn't sell me that for a, Latin motto, Heaven bless our home.' " A Delaware Justice has long enjoyed the reputation of being the ugliest specimen of humanity in the State. While out shooting he met a man so ill-looking that he levtlled his gun at him, observing, "Stranger, I swore ten years ago that if e ger I met a man uglier than my- self I'd shoot him, and you're the first I've come across." After rapidly surveying the Justice from head to foot, the pedestrian answered, Well, captain, if I look any worse than you do, shoot. I don't want to live any longer!" "How old would you take me to be, Mr. Snooks?" 'she lisped, looking unutterable things at him. "I dunno," he replied, twisting nervously about in his chair. I'm awfully old, I assure you. I've seen twenty-three sum- mers r "Then you ought to wear glasses," he replied, earnestly. "Why, Mr. Snooks? Glasses at twenty-three?" :" Yea: your eyestilit must be bad." I'm sure I don't know why you should think so," she pouted. "Because Fm afraid about twenty summers have gone by that you haven't seen." Don't live a single hour of your life without doing exactly what is to be done in it, and going straight through it from beginning to end. Work, play, study, whatever it is, take hold at once and finish it up squarely and cleanly. Then do the next thing, without letting any moments drop between. And, if you find yourself where you have so many things pressing you that you hardly know how to begin, let me tell you a secret: take hold of the first one that comes to hand, and you will find the I rest all fall into file and follow after like a eompany of well-drilled soldiers. "Maria," said the mistress of a Cans-avenue residence, as she entered the kitchen in a hurry the other day, "there's a man going out of the alley with a basket on his arm." " Yes'm." "I think he has stolen something . from the basement." "Oh, no, ma'am, I was watching him all the time." "But he had a basket of victuals.' "Yes'm but he's a poor man and I sympathised with him." "Haven't I told you not to feed tramps ?" 0 Yes'm, but he pleaded so hard." "Oh, they can all tell a pitiful story. Don't you ever give this man any- thing again. He looks to me like a State Prison bird." "Very well, ma'am. I'll tell him to keep away." "Then you know him?" Yes, he's my husband, and he's such a sweet talker, and he's so good-hearted." It. was at Kilravock (says Lord Cockburn) that old Henry Mackenzie used to tell that a sort of household officer was kept, whose duty it was to prevent the drunken guests from choking. Mackenzie was once at a festival there, towards the close of which the exhausted I topers sank gradually back and down on their chairs,: till little of them was seen above the table except their noses; and at last they disappeared altogether and fell on the floor. Those who were too far gone to rise lay there from necessity; while those who, like the Man of Feeling, were glad of a pretence for escaping, fell into a doze from policy. While Mackenzie was in this state, he was alarmed by feelings hand working about his throat, and called out. A voice answered, " Dinna be feared, sir, it's me." "And who are you?" " A'm the lad that louses the craavats." A King once said to his Minister, "Do you believe in luck?" "I do," said the Minister. "Can you prove it ?" said the King. "Yes; I can." So one night he tied up to the ceiling of a room a bag containing peas mixed with diamonds, and let in two men, one of whom believed in luck and the other in human efforts alone. The one who believed in luck quietly laid himself down on the ground, the other after a time found the bag and feeling in the dark the peas and stones, ate the peas and threw the diamonds ;to his companion, saying:" Therelare the stones for your idleness." The man below received them in his blanket. In the morning the King and Minister came and told each man to keep what he had found. The man who believed in trying got the peas which he had eaten, the other got the diamonds. The Minister then said: "Sire, there may be luck, but it is as rare as peas mixed with diamonsd; so let none hope to live by luck." Wtirrrien am) BURNS.—One day, when Whittier was about fifteen, there came a pedlar, an off-hand rhymer and ballad singer, who made use of his talents in showing his wares. He sang some of the songs of Burns, and the boy, for the first time in his life, knew the delight of music married to the sweetest songs ever written. An unimagined sense of beauty and melody was suddenly developed in his -heart and brain, Jim emotion was overpowering, as on the wings of song his aoul floated above his native valley. Thenceforth the boy lived a dual life; the murmur of music was in his ears, and the cadences of verse began to form in his teeming brain. The sight and sound of the farm became rhythmical, the sleigh-bells along the road in winter, the ring of whet- stones upon the scythes, the sweep of the mowers through the grass, the brook tinkling over the little cas- cades, the plaintive calls of whip-poor-wills at night, the hum pf the spinningrwheels, the roaring of the flies in the great chimney, and the wild anthem of the winds in the neighbouring woods. Then the visible universe became alive with meaning and analogy, and nature in all its forms filled him with an eager and passionate joy. About the same time the present from his schoolmaster of Burns's poems completed his happiness and determined bis careen—Good Wordq. [By WILKINS MACIWBER.I One cowd snowy mornin', a few weeks ago, I' one o' thoose black and darksome cooarts—at wi often read abeawt bu' varry seldum think o' visitin' —ther stood a dirty, unfurnished heawse, in which two little childer NMI fond half stem% an nearly naked, cryin' fur summat t'eat, while th' womanut they cawd mother wur drinkin' in th' vaults close by. Somb'dy wi' a bit o' feelin' abeawt em had bin tryin' t' get hur whoam, bur it wur aw no use; boo curst em fur ther pains, an' wi' a drunken leer ant em "wot they'd hay' t' sup?" " Missus," said a kind-hearted owd woman at had getten t' kno' wot wur th' matter, "do goo whoam ; th little things are clemmed fur summat t' eat, whoile yo're spendin' th' money drink Ileaw ved yo bike it yorsen' ? " " Wot th' " has it getten t' do thee? Mind th i own bisness, and spake wen theau'rt spok- ken to" an' wi' a bit ov a stagger boo went back agen into th' vaults. man instant aw picturCto mysen th, poor little childer at awd seen th' neet befooar trudgin' up an' deawn th', streets until nearly midneet, sellin' chips an' pappers, an' aw couldn't help thinkin' at th' ma- jority ov em wur bein' sacrificed at th' shrine ov Bacchus bi' ther drunken parents. Wot a strange fashionasion rink seeoms t' hay' fur sum foak Edrybody wur sayin' at trade wur bad an' money scarce, bu' it didn't look bike it bi th' way at they ke gooin' in an eawt o' th' gin shop. Early as it is they're quoite busy theere if nob'dy else is, an' bi th' mon, it's aw reddy money too. It wur awlus a quare thing to me at foak could find th' brass t' pay fur ther drink bu' fur owt else it's trust, trust, trust—aw'm towd at yo cawnt do any bisness beawt givin' trust, an' aw reckon it is so, bu' aw wonder heaw mony men,ay an' women too, hay' bin ruin't bi trustin' too much to th' honesty ov others. Yigh, ther's mony a mon at ud on'y bi too glad t'pay, bu' he cawnt, becos he foinds eawt when too late at he's fawn among thieves who've devoured' his livin' an' then bait him, as Shakespeer says, "to the mercy of a rude stream." Neawadays men seem t' be r sich a hurry t' ruin one another 'at if th' question wur put to -em " heaw yo bike it yorsen "it 'ud hay' abeautt as much effect as a flake o' snow droppin'l into a red hot fiery furnace. I Then thee are others 'at live as though this world's goods wur nobbut fur them, whoile th' rest Co' humanity wi' bits i' ther meawths an saddles on ther backs wur born fur them to ride, booted and spurred, roughshod, just wheerevvur they pleased. They'n bib playin at that game i' Ireland fur a lung toime neavr, and wi aw kno' th' result. Ev'ry sensibul mon admits I['at if ther'd on'y bin a bit moore charity an' not quoite so mich coershun, th' cry o' Rome Rule ud neyyur hay' bin uttered. Some foak are varry fond o' tellin' abeaut th' crimes an' th' outrages at hay' takken place r that unhappy country, bu' they nev-vur tab th' trubble t' foind eawt wot's bin th' cause ov em, fur even a worm I will turn when it's trodden on. Aw wonder wot 'they'd ha' done if they'd ha' bin turned eawto' ther heawses wi' a sickly woife an' a large family in th' middle o' winter, an' bait fur t' dee upo' th' road thro' no faut o' ther own? Aw darsay, if th' question wur put " Heavr ud yo bike in yorsen?" to thoose who are responsibul fur theese cruel pro- I ceedins, th' ansur ud varry loikely be as unfeelin'— I tho' praps a little moore refined—as that given hi' th' woman ut wur spendin' hur childers' bread i' drink. Th' good owd book tells us t' help one another, an' it does.:seeom strange r this great age ov pro- , fessin' Christians at sich good advice should be so mich neglected. Aw once yerd tell or a mon at wur woth his theausands, an' who took a varry prominent part f Church work, refusin' lend another Christian brother who happent to be a bit pressed a ten peawndnooat, an' yet a few days after th' same mon wur bein' praised sky-high fur havin' given ten theawsand peawund tooart buildin' a new church. When fortune smiles upon yo' an creawns ey'ry effort wi' success, yo're dignity 'll not suffer even then bi coomin' deawn a little t' help a poor strugglin' brother up th' hill o' bus. Ther's a good mony foak hay' ,getten a notion i' ther yeds at if they gie a hunclert or two tooart building a new church or chapel it 'll carry em straight throo' th' pearly gates, and bond em safe f Abram's buzzum.' Aw kno' toimes are bad, an' th' road 's bin varry rough an' uneven fur a mony foaks, bu' if errybody 'll do wot they con t' help one another, th' nch as well as th' poor, we shall poo throo' yet; at least, at's wot Ann Jane says, and awm o' th' same opinyun.

. . A YOYA.GE TO MELBOURNE.. . sickness. We shall cross the line towards night. The northern star seems to have disappeared, and a colonist BY RICHARD 'WYCLIFFE. I from Victoria told me he saw the southern cross the I Below is the continuation of the Journal kept by the whole of it last night. Whether he was mistaken or late Mr. Richard Rawcliffe, of Blackburn, during the ' not Ido not know. I know I looked for it very , voyage from London to Melbourne in the Orient Line diligently a long time but without success. As I sit ' here thousands of flying fishes I see glittering in the sun. Royal Mall Steamship Ga,ronne. The first portion of They are far more numerous than swallows over the the Diary appeared in last Saturday's Examiner fresh water ponds in thetold country on a warm June ' "Sunday, Sept. 12th.—I get down from my "bunk" as day. sore in the sides and chest as if I had swallowed knives "Monday. Sept. 27th.—We passed without ceremony the equatorial line about nine last nieht, so now we are and, through lying too long, I find I am too late to ge Imy day's supply of fresh water. I can,. however, ge some from some other fellow passenger. The scene here is magnificent.. We are going along in splendid weather past vineyards, orange groves, and land richly note that I'sent home another letter from Naples, which ~ "Monday, Sept. 13th.—Orders have just been given tct on palling in the southern hemisphere. -The morning is fine, and there is Scarcely a ripple in the Indian Ocean, but the sailors are taking down top tackle, preparing for stormy weather. I suppose, if all goes well, we shall cultivated through the straits of Messina. I forgot to arrive at Melbourne on Saturday, the 16th of October. ' Tuesday, Sept. 28th.—I have passed the night with our folks would not expect, not knowing we should have rather more comfort than I have before done since communication with land. coming aboard, on account of a good brisk trade wind having cooled the weather down a little. The wind still all passengers (3rd class) to bring their bedding up much enjoy the breeze, the sun, and the \ the top deck, and in a very short time all is hung which will fine scenery, on the Mediterranean.. I have just had a keeps fresh and brisk this morning, and I think we are I now more free from the sun's power. The day seems to with those necessary articles. No doubt the bugs, round I be ending as it began, with fine weather and a Stiff head are more numerous than the passengers who have paid wind. As I mate there is a large bird, called ' bo's'ain; their fare, wi hovering about the ship, and I yesterday saw one of the same kind. They fly like a gull, with wide outstretched chat with the doctor, as nice a gentleman as ever I met wings. Singular is their appearance so very far from with. I handed him an introductory letter land. I suppose they will live on fishes, and take rest on Bradford, of the Sbuthport Convalescent Hospital. He the waters. asked me if I was a steerage passenger, and I, in reply, , , (To be continued in our next,) told him I had an enclosed cabin berth, but that the food was same as steerage. I told him I could not, through being ill so long, raise the money necessary in order to come 2nd class. ," Was the food not suitable ?" "No," I said. "Then," said he, "I will order the steward to give you exceptional food, and come to me as often a& you think proper, for I shall be pleased, to do all I can for you." A squall set in about 3 p.m. The vessel began to rock, and I was soon laid down in " bunk " with sea Sickness. This sickness was again almost general with the passengers. "Tuesday, Sept. 14th.—Another fine morning, and the ship goes steady. I "Wednesday, Sept. 15th.—Fine weather and a calm sea. We arrived at Port Said at 1 p.m., but the captain ordered the hoisting of the yellow flag, and passengers were forbidden to go ashore, whicV was very annoying, for everyone about the ship were very soon as dirty as sweeps through the vessel taking in coal. What a lot of almostamde dirty-looking Arabs—about 200 in number —carrying off the coal in bags, and what a chattering noise they make! Well, we had to remain on board and receive the coal dust during a stoppage of 11 hours! The British ship Bengal, with the Duke of Connaught aboard, stained past us while we were anchored. The Garonne gave her a salute of 21 guns, and she was gaily dressed in bunting; and after the sun went down, two men of war, that were also anchored close to, were ex- pensively illuminated. The Duke was on his tour to India. Getting down in the berth, I managed—although the noises of the crew hoisting storage and articles of merchandise on board was something I had never ex- perienced before—to get sleep. ",Thursday, Sept. 16th.—To our surprise, our ship started off in the hours of early morning, and when I got on deck at 6 30 a.m., we had proceeded more than '3O miles up the Suez Canal. We were glad to have thus imperceptibly got out of the dirty port, and to find our- selves going along the narrow, calm canal. Naked Arab children followed us for miles after coppers. How they can run with expanded chest and head thrown back! Several pennies were thrown to them on the bank, but they were all lost in the desert sand. We saw just before breakfast a fox miming along the embankment. The weather is getting very warm, and we are troubled with the common fly, which bites very keenly. I have just performed anOther pleasing duty-. I have posted a letter —the last one until I arrive—for home. •It will, no doubt, be all the more welcome through being unexpec- ted, as neither Mrs. R. nor myself knew when I started on voyage that I should have the privilege of writing from any other place than Naples, if even from there. 4 p.m.—We are nearly through the Canal, but it seems the passengers will not be permitted to go ashore even here, as we seem to be in quarantine, floating the yellow flag. We have no cases of cholera aboard, but, through -ailing at Naples, which is to some extent infected, we are held to be not free from suspicion. "Friday; September 17th.—The ship has been stopped since 6 p.m. yesterday, waiting, so I am told, for the Mail. I, along with the passengers generally, would 'Much rather we went .along. Our vessel is the oldest, and, I believe, the slowest the company have. The berths are very small, and there is not near the space there ought to be to ensure the comfort of passengers. During the time we are anchored here many of the pas- sengers are occupied fishing, and seem on the whole suc- cessful, only what they do catch are only small ones, weighing about two or three ounces each, which, but for their very silvery appearance would look like English trout. The ship's crew have just hauled on board a young shark, 10ft. 61n., the first I have ever seen alive. I watched them cut him up, They first cut off his tail, and a deal of blood came from him. Then they opened his stomach which was almost empty, barring a lump of pork—the bait—he had swallowed, about three pounds in weight, which but for the hook attached would have been just a taste for him. The Austral, the finest vessel belonging to this line of Royal Mail Steamers, has just sailed up, homeward bound, and anchored close beside us. 1 p.m.—We have weighed anchor and are off again 'amid very hot weather. I shall never believe until I witness it that we shall have it much hotter. They have (at dinner) served out to each and all a dose of lime Juice. "Saturday, September 18th.—We have now 'got fairly into the Red Sea (I did not expect it being blue, but it is), and find the weather very hot. :I have for a time cast off my regular clothing, and wear thinner ones, and fewer of them. Drinking warm water add sweating seems the rule now. "Sunday, September 19th.—We have just about ar- rived At the Cancer tropic, and, barring allowances for the extreme heat, I feel no worse. My appetite I think has if anything improved. It is punishment to be com- pelled to fie in the "bunks," too, at 100 degrees tempera- ture, and I feel glad when the sun sends his golden beams through the portholes in the early morning. 4 p.m.—The heat is intense,for there is scarcely a breath of air. All have suffered, as there is a continuous sweating going on—even thoughwe had to cast off every stitch of clothing—all the day and night long. The sun has just disappeared behind the belt of deep waters, but still the heat is, maintained. At least two-thirds, of the passengers are pushing up the hatchway loaded with bedding, determined not to suffer AS they did last night, and are going to pass the night under no roof but that of "heaven's high vault." During the day six men were brought from below all but dead to all ap- pearance, from the heat. They were all ship's servants —young lads, barring a baker and a cook. The first man was the baker, and he, after breathing the air panted like a run-down hare. He, however, like the rest, recovered, though they have as yet not all got to work. "Monday, Sept. 20th.—I am still alive and kicking, as the saying is, thank God. I have so far stood the heat, and do not feel much weaker. Though the weather is hot, what little air we get is pure and strong. "Tuesday, Sept. 21st.—The doctor has just told me that he is surprised how well I am bearing up, and that I look better about the eyes. We had a visit paid us last evening by about a score of swallows; they alighted upon the awnings, ropes, &c., alternately, flying some distance away and back again. This morning Ido not see them. There is a little more breeze, but, though coming aft the vessel, it does little good. "Wednesday, Sept. 22nd.—We passed through' Hell's Gate' at eight last night. Contrary to expectation, we have not touched at Aden, and ar,e now scudding along through the Arabian Sea. The morning is pleasant enough on deck, but fearfully hot below. We have nearly all got what they call the prickly heat—a sort of , blood rash, not much unlike smallpox in appearance. Perhaps it is better out than in. Thoughts of home , keep stealing to my mind, its endearing associations, , my wife and family and friends I have left behind most dear to me, and also of those still dear to me—and especially at this time—in Australia. I pray: that I may beehls to get-to my future home improved in health. ‘"Thursday, Sept. 23rd.—The weather is somewhat cooler, but my general health Is much worse, and I can- not eat. We are being taken along the west coast of Africa, and are about half-way to Adelaide. "Saturday, Sept. 25th.—I have been sea-sick since I made my last note, and am very bad yet. We have had the sea quite as turbulent in the Indian Ocean as in the Bay of Biscay. I have just seen the doctor. He has givea me a tonic to strengthen me. I have been laid in .berth so long that the clothing is all wet with perspira- tion under me. My mate, Mr. Griffiths, from Lon- don, is very deaf, and he is always sick when I am, and we are often both in bed at the same time, so that we cannot help each other. This sea-sickness is bad to bear, but when coupledwith a wasting disease especially so. I often think of the couplet : ' Ye gentlemen of England, who live at home at ease, How little do ye dream about the dangers of the seas!' Byron says : ' I've seen your stormy seas and stormy women, But I pity husbands rather more than seamen.' Of course his lordship must have been an exception to the generality of men in his ideas of married life, as more men enter into the married state than go to sea. Theie seems to be a good deal of ' growling ' about the 'grub,' and, indeed, there is much occasion for it. One gentleman from Yorkshire 'fitted up' one of the stewards pretty well. At his table they were complaining when 'Mac.,' one of the stewards, says, 'Hold your tongues ! , You're like a lot o' pigs l' 'We are pigs, theaw knows that,' says the . Yorkshire- man,' or theaw'd nod bring us pig stuff to heyt l' The sea is now much calmer than it has been forseveraldays, and the weather warmer. We are expected to cross the line towards Monday if all goes well. lam sure there is not a man; woman, or child aboard the GaTORDO but wishes heartily that he or she was safely landed at Mel- bourne, Sydney, or whatever port be their destination. Bad as I am, Ido pity the women who -have one, two, and some of them three children with them. "Sunday, Sept. 28th, 7 a.m.—l was up early this morning, for I am already washed, have changed - linen, and am passing my time looking over the -ship's side. The morning is very, fine and pleasant, the sea calm. I cannot bear a rocking ship, and I feel, I cannot say that 'Richard is himself again,' but I feel free from sea

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. ALLUS TEK THINGS AS THEY CUM. Ther's sum fooak uts allus on't grumble When th' air's full o't fragrance o' pooasies; An' they'll chunner an' jabber, an' mumble, When th' cowd drop's on th' ends o' ther nooases. This world's wrong, it ne'er con be reighted, To snarlers uts crusty an' glum; It's ther own faut, they feel o'erweighted, They mun lam n to tek things as they cum! It's th' same, whether playin' or workilf. They cackle like hens on for layin' WP ther' waggin' jaws, snappin' an' jerkin, They will shove ther nasty cowd " say " in. They're fidgety an' discontented, I An, cross-grained as owd knock-kneed 'rum; An' gradely fooak think 'em demented, 'Cause they never tek things as they cum! Ther's some fooak 'll smash comfort i' finders, Wi' hearts in a flutter wi' frettin', An' they ceawer wi' e'en fixed among t' cinders,— Th' bonny blue sky aboon they're forgettin', While they mope cea,wntin' up o ther troubles, Like skoo-lads sooar plagued wi' a sum. Poor foos ! they cud brast o Care's bubbles, If they'd stan', and tek things as they cum! What's th' use ov a chap sick an' seedy, Allus keepin' his brain on to th' moyther ? Id meks him look clammed, ill, an' needy, An' he shrivels up like a deead spider. Yet, aw know lots misel as 11 study Till tber heyds ged booath heavy an' numb. Dom'd rake t Match, an' mek t' watter muddy, Let id be, an' tek things as they cum! If care thumps at yor door, let id tarry, Turn th' key reawnd, dornd let id cum inwart, We've o big looads o' trouble to carry Bud wise men put up wee't an' grin oer't. A good hearty laff, an clear conshunce, , Are signs ov a life, welly plumb, Contentments P th' cot mooar than manshuns, Keep id theer, an' tek things as they corn! If yor gaffer an yo conned hit id Thro' his hard tyranizin' an jewin ; Dornd think as bi good men yor pitied, Yo mun better yorsel, or face ruin. For when he's done his toast to ced o'er yo He'll leave yo yor fingers an'bthumb • A good hand meks good brass; th' worlds afoor yo, Jack up streyt ! an' tek things as they cum! If yo've nice chubby childer reawnd tlatable, As nibble away yo'r toil-treasure, Yo've th' odds o' thoose beawt, for yor able To see every face beeam wi pleashur, If yo've getten full steeom on to muster, Woci'lljust buy o th' chelpers a crumb, An' thers THREE mooar cums o ov a cluster, Whistle low, an' tek things as they cum! Thers a good decal th' knowledge o Science For o men, fro th' weyver to th' farmer; But tilers mooar in a sturdy reliance, For th' heart an' forth' mind its th' best armour, Wi thad, yo'll nod dawdle i' th' blue uns, When you hear th' momin' buzzer's long hum! PRESENTATION TO 'ME REV. S. • WILKINSON.

On Saturday evening a social gathering was held in the Infant Schools, Heath-side, at which the , Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's Church, War- I rington, was presented with a timepiece,with cande- I lebra to match. The Rev. R. Wood Samuel (curate) presided, and among those present, in addition to ' the vicar, were Mrs. Wilkinson, Miss Wilkinson, the Rev. G. D. Wray (vicar of St. Peter's), Mr. Turner, Mr. Thomas Jolley, Mr. and Mrs. James Smethurst, Mr. A. Jolley, Mr. and Mrs. Pollitt, Mr. C. , Ashurst, Mr. James H. Smethurst, . Mr. Parkinson, Mr. Plinston, and Mr. Fryer. A pianoforte solo, "The Battle of Prague," having been played by Miss M. Smethurst, songs were given by Miss Locker, Miss Oxley, and Messrs. Parkinson, Bellian (comic), Hill and Fryer, Mr. George Riley and Mr. Parkinson officiating as accompanists.— The presentation was made by Mr. A. JOLLY (su- perintendent of the boys' school), who said that in many parishes besides their own there were classes somewhat like that over which for so many years their vicar jutd presided, but he was quite confident that in no parish was there a better feeling exist- ing between teacher and class than in that at St. Paul's parish. (Hear. hear, and applause.) There was one special point which he must not forget to mention. The presentation which was about to be made was intended to take the form of a birthday gift to the vicar, but as Mn Wilkinson's birthday occurred in Lent, and it was desired there should be a little social gathering accompanying it, it was de- cided to meet earlier in the month than they other- wise would have done. However, that could not be very well avoided. The class in question was prac- tically a men's Bible class, but it had been known for many years as the first class in the boys' school. The manner in which tliat testimonial had been got up was beyond all praise. It was the spontaneous offering of the vicar's own class, and no outsider had had a part in it. He trusted Mr. Wilkinson would accept that gift—and he was .'speaking as the mouthpiece of the class—not merely as an ex- pression of the kind and warm feeling which had existed for many years towards him, but as an ear- nest of their strong desire that their connection with him might not be severe formanyy ears. (Applause.) —The Rev. S. WILKINSON, having warmly acknow- ledged the gift, said a clergyman's life was an arduous and a difficult one; if he did his duty in the sight of God and man he must be continually employed in the work of the ministry, and con- tinually giving his thoughts and attention to it. It seemed to him that a clergyman's work consisted of several divisions. In the ,first place, there was the private study which every man ought to give to his work. Mr. Jolley had alluded to certain feelings, sentiments, and ideas, which were now to a great extent occupying the minds of thinking men of the present day. Therefore, a clergyman ought, if he wished to be a true minister of Christ, to study as much as he could the objections and the difficulties which were urged against the Christian faith. He knew that it was a very easy matter to talk in that way, but it was a much more difficult ' thing to act, because those studies were very diffi- cult, and many of them had not the time or learn- ing to carry them out as they ought. At the same time, if a clergyman wished to benefit his people, , as well as do himself justice, he must give as much tune as he possibly could to reading. There were also the public ministrations of religion to which he had to attend—the services on the Lord's Day and during the week. Another duty was the visi- tation of the sick. It was a good thing for a clergyman to go as often as he could hAo the schools on week days, and take a class in the Old or New Testament or their excellent Church of England catechism, and there instil those duties to man which they had to carry out in their life as children and adults. (Applause.) He had in his class many who, he hoped, would be future town councillors and Mayors of Warrington, and he urged them if ever they were elected mem- bers of the Council to put a stop to Sunday funerals, which were very good in their way, but now that they had the Saturday half-holiday they might all be held on that day. He could speak from his own experience, and on behalf of his clerical friends, that Sunday funerals did interfere i tremendously with the work n the Sunday school. '(Applause.) During the time he had been in War- rington, he had spent 15 of the happiest years in his life, because he believed that his dear wife and himself, as well as Miss Wilkinson—(applause)— and she was a Sunday school teacher were sur- rounded by,lgying fellow-workers. He trusted they were all working lot one object. namely, the ad- vancement of God's cause amongst men. (Ap- plause.)—The remainder of the evening as spent in an enjoyable manner.
MR. JOSEPH HOWES LECTURES.
"IRELAND AND 11011 E RULE." 2 This formed the title of the fifth and last lecture of

the series of addresses on political topics by Mr, Joseph Howes under the auspices of the Warrington Liberal Association, and was given in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Friday night week. There was a very large and enthusiastic: audience, the ;oom being crowded. The chair was occupied by Dr. J. H. Gornall, J.P., who was supported by the Rev. Father Carew, Messrs H. Roberts, C. S. Burgess, F. Lough-, lin, W. Pierpoirtt, E. Whitehead, George Walker, Ti Birchall, Yolin Bromley, S. Dunbobbin, W. Crosskill, J. McConville, J. Mounfield jun., 'l'. Flood, J. Evans, B. Roberts.

The CHAIRMAN' who was warmly received congrat- ulated them upon that great meeting, and proceeded to say that in May, 1885 some of the leaders Of the Irish National Party entered into a conclave with re- iTonsible members of the Tory Party, who Were then in opposition, to oppose any renewal of any pertion of the Crimes Act. The information 'WU, kept secret from Lord Spencer who was then her Majesty's re, presentative in Dublin, and members of the Tory Party who ultimately became members of Lord Salis- bury's Government of that year, openly denounced the Ulster Tories as reactionary when they defended Lord Speneer, He (Dr. Gornall) trusted the hives of tee Irish would never be satisfied until they had ob- tained a domestic legislature of their own, (Ap- plause), though they still believed in the necessity of maintaining these islands as one kingdom under one crown. lie quoted words of Mr. Gladstone when he,l said that they merely sought the' settlement of that great question, and considering that much of the I peace, and happiness which England and Scotland en- I )(sped was due to Liberal legislation there could be no better celebration Of Her Majesty's Jubilee than by acknowledging the abstract claims of Ireland to self-guvernment (aeplauso), and proceeded to say that the appeal to the country last year was temporarily fatal to Mr. Gladstone's measure,and he would ask through whom? Not their old enemies the Tories, but to a section of their own party described by Lord Randolph Churchill as a crutcn to be thrown away when no longer reqoired (laugh- ter and apt Luse). He (the chairman) said at the Liberal Club the other day that as a party they were made to differ and honest differences were a provision for assuring the ad- vance of meta towards a nobler political life, but was it not possible that in attempting to retain this small section they were paying far too high a price? 'Whoa the question of Home Rule was settled on the lines of Mr. Gladstone's bill, as settled it would be, be phould like to ask the representa- tives of the "Crutch," were. they, going to desert them when the disestablishinent of the state Church came to the front, or when the power to limit Use baneful influence of the drink traffic was within their grasp, and on whatever the great Tory depended for sustenance and physical life. His opinion was that the Groschenites and Hartingtenians were shaking on many more subjects than 'ldome Rule. (Applause). Mr. Howes would tell them thati their cause was a prospect of happier days for Ireland, and he (the chairman, thought he:might say in their name that as Radi- cals they intended Le wore perhaps not for an easy but 'a certain and not far distant victory. (Applause). Mr. HowEs then proceeded with his lecture. He briefly reviewed his remarks on the subject of Home Rule and Ire- land at the previous lectures, and said that as that was the subject upon which the next election would turn, and if the question was not then settled, upon whatever the following election wcaild turn, they must keep on repeating the argu- ments until they had gotthem fairly rivetted upon the pub- lic.miud. He said the extension of the franchise gave the people an opportunity of asking for what they wanted and the Irish people had availed themselves of the opportunity. Mr. Gladstone introduced his bills for grappling with the difficulty, and the present crisis was due to seceding Liber- als, who had no followers, and who were beginning to lose favour in their position. He urged that Horne Rule meant that people should manage their own affairs (applause),and home rule being right in principle it was good for the fami- ly, good for the locality, and good for the country. (Ap- plause.) Ireland had never been treated as a sister country but as a conquered counrty and the iron heel of the oppressor had been ground into the very souls of the oppressed. Home Rule the talk of to-day would be an accomplished fact to-morrow and it was aleo a fact that before long there would be a Parliament in Ireland, that would enable the Irish people to manage their own aff iirs according to their own ideas. (Applause). The present home rule scheme was the opening out of a great home rule scheme, which would have to be extended to a far greater extent before the business of the Empire could be properly managed. (Applause.) He urged there should be separate Parliaments in Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, for affairs purely concerning those countries, with a true Im- perial Parliament in this country for Imperial matters, and then they would have a much better state of things than had ever existed in this csantry up to the present. (Ap- plause.) Home Rule was a system of trusting the people, of liberating the peclple, and of a general emancipation for the people who. were straggling for it. ( Applause.) He referred at some length to the details of Mr. Gladstone's measure, and combatted various arguments used against it. In concluding, he urged them to flapped that great measure of justice, and said if they were going to do justice to Ire- land let them go about it in a proper manner—(applause)— for Home Rule for Ireland would be a step in the right direction, and would tend to bring about the consolidation of the Empire, and increase the happiness of the people. (Cheers.) Mr. THOMAS FLOOD (a working man), in moving .a vote of thanks to I1(r. Howes for his address, urged that Irish- men should bh trusted with Home Role.' They merely claimed to be placed on an equality with the other people of the Empire. (Applause..)—Mr. C. S. BURGESS, in second- ing the motion, said be considered it was the duty of. every Englishman to help forward that scheme of justice to Ire- land, and as the next election would turn upon the subject they should endeavour to educate the people. (Applause.)— Mr. F. LOUGHLIN supported the motion, and said the pass- ing of the Home Rule Bill of Mr. Gladstone would be the dawning of a brighter era for Ireland and for this coantry. (Applause.) The motion was carried, sand a similar compliment to the chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: HORRIBLE BURNING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: HORRIBLE BURNING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.

Between ten and eleven o'clock on Saturday night, Margaret Hackett, a widow' fifty-six years of age, who lived at 91, Atlas-court, Parr-street, met with her death under extraordinary and horrible circumstances. Deceased lodged with a waft named Cawley and his wife, and her three brothers' John, Peter, and Francis, all middle-aged men, lived with their mar- ried sister, Ann Lyon, at 66, Parr-street. About nine o'clock on Saturday night deceased proceeded to their house, and found Ann Lyon, John, au cl Peter in. Uncertainty prevails as to what followed, until about a quarter to eleven a woman named Tobin ob- served smoke issuing from the front door of the house, which was open. She raised an alarm, and several persons who entered met with a shocking spectacle. Hrs. Hacket was lying on the kitchen floor, with her clothes burning and smouldering. Afrer the flames had been extinguished, it was found that the woman was dead, that all her clothing had been burnt, and the body literally roasted. The arms and legs were different shapes, and the fingers almost entirely burnt off. Immediately after the brother John was was discovered on the stairs, also shockingly burnt. Inspector Whittaker, Sergeant Gilligan, and Constables Ratcliffe and Moffatt mere soon on the scene, as were also Mr. W. J Mooney, of Traverse-street (chemist at the Hard- shaw Brook Chemical Works), Mr. Joynson (assistant to Dr. M`Nicoll), and Mr. Stewatt (relieving offic.er). Every assistance was rendered to the injured man, and after his wounds had been dressed he WAS taken to the Providence Hospital. The Borough Fire Brigade shortly afterwards arrived for the purpose of extinguishing the fire in the house. but this had been accomplished by buckets of water, and the body of the woman was laid out in the front room. It is stated that the deceased had not been Well for a few weeks, and had sedmed low-spirited, and in the coarse of conversation with a neighbour on Saturday afternoon re- marked that if anything should happen to her that night would she see her washed and laid out, as she felt she could not live long. No one appears to know how the woman got on fire.— Joha Connor, who WAS removed to the hospital, has stated that he left the house some time after his brother, and on returning found his sister all in flames. Ho pulled off his coat and threw it around her, but did not remember what followed, nor how he got into the neighbour's house. John's coat was almost totally consumed, and a washing tub in the room was half burned away. The back door, too, was badly scorched and blistered by the fire. An inquest on the body of the deceased was opened before Mr. S. Brighouse, coronet, at the Lion Hotel, Higher Parr-street, on Monday. Evidence having been given, a Juror remarked that so one seemed to know anything about how it happened.—The Coroner observed that that was all the evidence they could have upon the case and it was for the jury to return a verdict upon what they had beard. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

TEE Lunacy- L•ws.—ln discussing an amendment the LORD CHANCBLLOR said he could not consent to leave the whole matter of confinement of a lunatic in the hands of medical men. It was necessary that some judicial authority should intervene, therefore if the principle of the clause was admitted—that the person accused, so to speak, of lunacy should have a right to demand to be brought before a magistrate,—the subsections should be remodelled. On the motion of the LORD CHANCELLOR, new clauses were agreed to ambling the Lord Chancellor to supersede the inquisition, and rescind or vary the order for the commitment of a lunatic to an asylum on satisfactory evidence being given of the cure of such lunatic. The bill passed committee. Their lordships adjourned at 6 5 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Monnev.

Armin= Renwar.—The proposal of Mr. Bryce to instruct the Committee on the Ambleside Railway Bill to inquire whether the proposed railway would interfere with the enjoyment of the public, and to receive evidence, was considered at some length, and the debate was adjourned to Thursday. Empr.—ln reply to questions, Sir J. FERCSISSON said the proposals made by the Government did not include a withdrawal of British troops from Egypt as long as there was any doubt as to the Egyptian Government maintaining itself. The Government was well aware of the difference between Belgium and Egypt. SIR THOMAS ESMONDE, M.P., DEFYING THE CROWN.— Mr. T. W. RUSSELL asked the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether the Sir T. Esmonde, recently appointed High Sheriff of the county of Waterford, was the same gentle- man as described in the Pall Mall Gazette as engaged in defying the authorities, and what steps her Majesty's Government proposed to take? (Ministerial cheers.)— Mr. T. P. O'Coangon : Before the right hon, baronet replies, I would ask him whether he will adhere in this case to the rule he laid down in another case, viz., not to answer a question in the absence of the person referred ? (Hear, hear.)—Sir M. HICKS BEACH: I did not lay down any such rule. What I protested against was a question being asked without notice by an hon. member. lam not disposed to take for granted every item of intelligence which appears in the Pall Mall Gazette. (Laughter and "Hear, hear.") In this matter I may say that the action of Sir Thomas Esmonde, with reference to the appointment of a sub-sheriff, has been already brought under the notice of the Lord Chancellor, and if this paragraph be true there will be no delay in dealing with the matter. (Ministerial cheers)._

THE CoLuKar Disasvan IN Souvia WALES.—In answer to Mr. Tomlinson, Mr. MATTHEWS said the last telegram from the scene of the colliery disaster in South Wales stated, he was sorry to say, that 37 lives had been lost. Nineteen bodies had been brought up. There was difl7 culty in recovering the remaining bodies until ventilation had been restored.

RECEPTION OF MR. SLAGG.—Mr. John Stagg, who was introduced by Mr. Arnold Morley and Sir Ughtred Kay- Shuttleworth, took the oath and his seat for Burnley, in the place of Mr. Rylands, deceased. The hon. member was received with loud and prolonged Opposition cheers.

div.head: RULES OF PROCEDURE.
div.p: THE RULES OF PROCEDURE.

Mr. W. H. Surrfr rose to submit the first of the pro- posed rules of procedure : That at any time after a question has been proposed a motion may be made, if the consent of the Chair has been previously obtained, "That the question be now put." Such motion shall be put forthwith, and decided without amendment or'debate. When the motion "That the question be now put" has been carried, and the question consequent thereon has been decided, any further motion may be made (the consent of the Chair having been previously obtained) which may be requisite to bring to a decision any question already proposed from the Chair; and also if a clause .be then under consideration, a motion may be made (with the consent of the Chair as afore- said) that the question, That the clause stand part of, or be added to, the bill, be now put. Such motions shall be put forthwith, and decided without amendment or debate. Pro- vided always, that questions for the closure of debate shall not be decided in the affirmative, if a division be taken, unless it shall appear by the numbers declared from the Chair that such motion was supported by more than 200 members, or was opposed by less than 40 members, and supported by more than 100 members. . _

Mr. Smith made some general observations on the plan as a whole, and, replying to the criticisms on its inade- quacy, he said he was extremely unwilling to put any restraint at all on private members, and that, though it might be possible to strengthen the Rules hereafter, it would not be so easy to retreat from them. In regard to the new closure, the Speaker, he pointed out, though no longer responsible for putting it into operation, would have a discretion in the matter. But he added that new changes in the Rules would be of no advantage unless members practised self-restraint tvith regard to the length and number of their speeches. Mr. GrAnsrroNE thought it was idle for the Government to expect to relieve the House of its difficulties by means of merely penal, restrictive, or repressive measures, and be- lieved that more success was to be expected from a large and frank proposal of devolution than by any change in the mode of conducting the debates. He thought the pro- posal of the Government was totally ioadeqsate, and that there was not the smallest chance of it producing any real effect on the increasing mass of business that the House now bad to do. _ _

The debate was continued by Mr Parnell, Mr Whitbread, Mr Chaplin, Mr Gill, Mr Craig-Sellar, Mr Salt, Mr A O'Con- nor, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Sir W Har- court; and it was adjourned on the motion of Sir Lyon Playf air. I The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past one o'clock.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. TIM RELEASE OF PRISONERS IN INDIA—The Earl of DERBY asked for information in relation to the release of 25,000 prisoners in India in honour of the Queen's Jubilee, remarking that if the prisoners had undergone adequate punishment they ought to be released whether there was a jnilee or not, and if they had not it was hardly expedient to set them free merely to give eclat to a public celebration.— LordCaoss said the Viceroy had not acted without great consideration, or without consultation with his advisers in India. The Viceroy had telegraphed that 23,007 criminal and 298 civil prisoners had been released, and that the measure was most acceptable to native sentimant, and supported by the practice of native rule.—The subject then dropped. Their Lordships adjourned at five minutes to five o'clock.

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. A QUESTION or PRIVILEGE—Sir W. Laws,w, calling attention to an article in the "Times " reflecting on the Irish members, which he thought was a reflection on the House asked if he would be in order in moving a resolution on the etatement.—The SPEAKER ruled that, however grave the imputations and charges in the article, it was not a case of privilege, and therefore n) discussion could take place. PaocaoonE.—The debate on the first of the proposed Rules of Procedure was resumed by Sir L. PLAYFAIR, who asked the House to give serious consideration to the propo- sal that instead of the Speaker being the interpreter of the evident sense of the House, an ordinary member was to take the initiative, and that the consent of the Speaker was then to be obtained.—Sir J. MownuaY thought the Government had done wisely in confining their recommen- dations of devolution to two Committees, but he did not re- gard the proposals of the Government with any sanguine expectations.—Lord HARTINGTON hoped the effect of adop- ting the rules about to be considered might be in the direction of somewhat shortening debates and speeches. He doubted whether they were saving time by the preliminary discussion. He scarcely thought the system of Grand Committees proposed by Mr. Gladstone had yet had a fair , trial, and in his opinion the proposals of the Government would not in any sense constitute a rejection or even a per- manent postponement of the principle of devolution.—Mr. Osborne Morgan, Mr. H. H. Howorth, Mr. F. S. Powell, and other hen. members continued the debate, which was again adjourned. Elm BlLLS—Leave was given to Mr. Mundella to bring in a bill to amend the law relating to the fraudulent mark- ing of merchandise, and to Mr. Jackson to bring in a bill to amend the Act relating to County Courts, and to provide for the sanitary rezistration of bdildings. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. _ _

The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes past two o'clock. THE DEBATE ON PEOCEDURE.—MT. FLYNN resumed the adjeurned debate on the rules of procedure, and contended that if a large system of devolution could be obtained there was no necessity for the closure rule.—Mr. DE LISLE was so impressed with the evil df so much talk that he thought the proposals of the Government deserved the hearty support of all.—Mr. LABOIICHERE doubted whether these rules would really shorten the debate.—After some remarks from Mr. IL Fowler and Sir R. Knightley, Mr. RITCHIE said the Govern- ment bad every reason to be satisfied with the conciliatory nature of the discussion, which showed every disposition to assist the Government. The Goveragnent had no desire to fetter freedom of debate in the Rouse, bat to imprdve and make effective the rule passed in 1882.—Mr. Illingworth, Mr. W. M•Donald, Mr. Ambrose, and Mr. J. O'Connor fol- lowed. The latter member continued his observations tilt a quarter to six, when, by the standing order, the debate was adjourned. BILL WITHDRAWIC—The Free Libraries Act Conzolida- lion Bill was withdrawn, and the House adjourned at ten minute to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TsunsnAv.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter after four o'clock. MiSaLLANEOUS.—The Lords diecussed Lord BRAMWELL'S Law of Evidence Amendment Bill, the object et which is to allow persons charged with crime to give evidence on their biol.—The Marquis of SALISBURY approved of the proposed change in the law, and the bill was read a second time. —Lord Butnrwsu, then moved the second reading of a bill which will allow magistrates at their option to send cases of burglary to quarter sessions for trial, instead of to assizes.— Tbe bill woo read a second time. MTThEUM FREE LECTURES. The fourth of the series of these free lectures was g.iven in the Lecture-room at the Museum, on Mon- day evening, by Mr. Hedley Fitton; subject. "J. M. W. Turner, H.A.. and his works". In the absence of Mr. W Owen, through indisposition, Alderman Webster presided, and in introducing Mr. Fitton re- marked that no doubt many of thenilmew that Turn- er had occupied the thoughts of some of the worthi- est and cleverest men England, and in fact the wotld, had produced. His works had been the un- failing theme of contrOversy,being by many consid- ered to surpass those of almost every other artist, whilst by others they were considered to fall far short. It however could not be controverted that many of Turner's works had not been surpassed by any artist since the world began, s though no doubt the differences of opinion would continue, and, as they knew, some of Turner's pictures had been painted at a time when the mechanical skill, of the artist was diminished by age. (Applause). Mr. Fitton then gave his lecture. He said that in the year 1843, John Ruskin published a book called os- tensibly. "Modern Painters," but which was really a glorification of the works and genius of a veteran artist.—Joseph William Mallord Turner. In it he first argued that no man can be appreciated proper- ly but by his equals or superiors and that gener- al public opinion Is no criterion of the worth of a man and his doings except after long intervals of time. Unfortunately, the cry of the young champ- ion came too late for the eloquent voice which could translate into such glowing language the dumb poetry of Turner's pictures had scarcely made the air of England thrill with its musical enthusiasm when a aloud black as night fell upon the aged painter and the glorious sun of his genius disap- peared without any twilight; he was dead as an artist and dying as a man. The life of Turner had been from beginning to end one series of grand and glorious revelations. ' Beauty after beauty had been revealed to men's astonished. 'eyes. Nature had been ransacked and her choices treasures displayed to the ken of the world. Effects that mortal man had seen and yet not seen were depicted with the magical strength and fidelity of a masuer-mind, until the, art world gazed with wonder, unable to grasp the massive accumulation of facts, unable to compre- hend the truths so new, so startling, so unheard of, that glowed year after year from the production of his genius. That a man like Turner should have been so little understood was not to be wondered at. He overthrew all preconceived notions of what was right in art, and ruthlessly destroyed the golden images which painters almost from time im- memorial had set up, not from obstinacy, but from a thorough conviction that in what he had learnt from nature, and sought to teach men his prin- ciples were right. The old masters had almost in- variably interpreted the beauties of nature by blues, greys, and browns. In everything almost they attempted to depict, the " brown demon" was brought into requisition; everything must have in it its quota of brown. Turner overthrew these no- tions; gave to his productions the actual relative colours of nature, "gave to the cataract its iris, to the sea its intense azure, gave to the sky its clearest gold," and decked the earth in its own sweet hues. That such revolutions should evoke considerable hostility was natural. Men cannot bear their pet schemes and notions to be rudely set upon one side; but time has done its work, and thousands pay reverential homage to the man, who, without doubt, may be styled the greatest landscape painter the world has ever seen. Referring to Turner's earlier days, Mr. Fitton said that at this period of his life, Turner became greatly enamoured of the hills and vales of Yorkshire, and it is to the broad wooded steeps and swell of the Yorkshire downs that 'we owe the singular massiveness in Turner's mountain drawing, and which gives it one of its chief elements of grandeur. Those who have seen much of Yorkshire would perceive how true that was. In most of his works there was something of• Yorkshire in them. Other artists were led away by foreign quaintness, but Turner's regard for home scenery always predominated. It had been said that Turner was the greatest master of foliage in lEurope. This was open to dispute, but in all other things in nature he seemed to have had a perfect mastery over the sky' at early morn, at midday, and at eve; , over the mountains, the undulating hills, the greenl pastures, leafy dells, and weedy foregrounds. There Turner stands upon an eminence from which he looks back over the universe of God, and we approach his works not to be pleased, but to be taught, and not to forn a judgment, but to receive a lesson." hen Turner was 23 he painted a pic- ture called "Morning amongst the Coniston Fells." This picture—an atmospheric effect—foreshadowed what afterwards Constituted the great charm in the majority of his works. To it he appended a poeti- cal quotation from Milton, and it might be noticed that to almost every picture aftet this he appended some poetical descriptioif. Many of these were his own, and if the painter-poet understood their meaning no one else did. (Laughter.) He spoke of the setting sun as being

Ephemeral as the summer fly Which rises, flits, expands, and dies. A comparison of the sun to a fly, or to a fly expand- , ing, was certainly a fall from the sublime to the ' ridiculous. (Laughter.) In another poetical effu- sion the struggling versifier introduces Bridport rather practically to is, as • The low sunk town from early time Remarkable for thread called Bridport twine. (Laughter.) There ' was hardly much hope for a poet so helpless, as Turner was in the use of words, and who could not even spell correctly, but he felt poetry and painted poetry, though he could not write it. It would be wearisome to enumerate the pictures of the period between the ages of 25 and 45, which marked the dawn of Turner's genius. They might be passed with the remark that they were painted in the style of the old masters, gloomy, with little colour, and conven- tional, yet showing at the same time great power. Throughout this period Turner had worked in rivalry of Claude, and was little more than an imitator; but at the age Qf 45 he entered upon a career perfectly original. From this time up to the age of 60 might well be termed a period of light, for it was then that those charming pictures, full of lovely colour, and replete with poetical feeling, I startled the world. Italy seemed to have brought i about a great change n Turner. He literally revelled in the glorious colours of Venice, and it is , in these Venetian pictures of Turner that his great powers of mystery and poetry are most evident. His Venetian pictures had been adversely criticised. He was accused of exaggerating the colour, and giving fictitious representations of this his favourite subject. But from surpassing the glories of Venice he fell short of them. Compare • one of his works with nature, and it would be as dull clay to bur nished gold and silver. The fact was Turner com- pressed.into his works many more truths of colour than most persons could perceive in one scene, and it was through want of perception that Turner was so much abused. Ruskin said that "The greatest artist is he who has embodied in the sum of his works the greatest number of the greatest ideas," and ac- cording to this definition Turner must be considered the greatest landscape painter, for his works convey the greatest number of the greatest ideas. (Ap- plause.) In the course of his lecture Mr. Fitton gave many interesting detals with regard to Tur- ner's works, the qualities of which were further illustrated by a number of copies of the more famous pictures that were handed round. It should be mentioned that there was again a full' attend- ance.

'BURNLEY ELECTION.-TRIUMPHANT N
RETURN OF MR. SLAG-.

One of the fiercest electoral struggles that has ever agitated the town of Burnley terminated on Saturday night in a great victory for the Liberal party, Mr. John Slagg being returned with the eminently satisfactory majority of 545 over the local Conservative candidate, Mr. J. 0. S. Thursby. The more sanguine members of the Liberal party never expected a greater majority than 200. The Conservatives, continuing their coalition with some of the Liberal Unionists who supported the late Mr. Peter Rylands, and returned him by a majority of 43 at the election in July, were unable to induce Sir Geo. Trevelyan to enter the lists as a Liberal-Unionist candidate, and accordingly fell back on Mr. J. 0. S. Thursby, a young gentleman, to whose quali- fications of docile adherence to tie stern nega- tive Irish policy of Lord Salisbury was added the good fighting attribute of local connection with the town of Burnley and the chief mining industries of the district. On the other hand, Mr. Slagg was fortified with the mature judgment that comes of long experience in industrial pursuits and commercial enterprise; he brought with him a noble record of ser- vices rendered on behalf of his country in the cause of freedom of commerce and the educational equipment of our industrial communities; and he unfolded a pro- gramme of reforms which have long been dear to the hearts of the Burnley Liberals, but which were impos- sible of achievement while the Irish question remained unsettled. The solution of the difficulty was the grant- ing of Home Rule to Ireland, which he believed would produce peace, good-will, order, and esteem, and tend to the greater solidarity ot the empire. Though braced with the epistolary assistance of Lord Harting- ton, the temperament of the Conservative managers in Burnley was throughout the week far from being char- acterised by that brisk hopefulness which led them cheerily to the support of the late Mr. Peter Rylands. There was a haunting fear that many of the dissentient Liberals would strain a point to vote for a Liberal Union- ist like the late Mr. Rylands, but would utterly scorn the 'idea of voting for a man pledged to the maintenance of the uncompromising tenets of the old Tory school. The Rev. J. E. Barton, a Baptist minister, who voted for Mr. Rylands at the last election publicly returned to the Liberal fold and acted as chairman at one or two of Mr. Slagg's meetings. His action was simply representative of the prevailing temper among the rank and file of those who had been regarded as Liberal dissentients. The Conservatives, alarmed at these symptoms, and justly fearing the consequences of a declaration of another Liberal Unionist that the prin- ciples then on trial were concretely Liberalism v. Tory- ism, tried to re-animate their own section with the invention Of 700 "men in buckram,”—good Conservatives who could not Conscientiously sacrifice their votes at the Liberal Unionist altar last year, but who would, of course, now place their offerings unreservedly at the feet of Mr Thursby. Some Dissentient Liberals, holding a promi- nent position ,in Burnley, also stood out. • and appended their names to a manifesto comfirming their previous resolutions. To strengthen the Unionist cause in this desperate crisis the town was placarded with the most earnest appeals to the electors to main- tain the unity of the empire, and Mr. T. W. Russell, M,P. for South Tyrone, Colonel Saunderson, the leader of the Loyalist party in Ireland, Sir H. Fergusson, and others opened fire on the Gladstonian ranks. The attack was repelled by Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., and the Right Hon. J. Stansfeld, M.P., before whose destruttive criticism the case as put forward by the Unionists fell like a house of cards. The Right Hon. Sir U. X. Shuttleworth, M.P., cleared the somewhat murky atmosphere with a plain, judicial account of the issues before the constituency, and when Sir Wilfrid Lawson closed the platform cam- paign the hearts of Mr. Slagg's supporters were "bound- ing with high hope." Mr. Slagg's canvass was exceed- ingly satisfactory, and on the morning of the election day his return was generally considered certain, the only dispute being as to his majority. The poll closed at eight o'clock, and shortly after that hour the ballot boxes were removed to the Mechanics' Institution where a large crowd had assembled. The Mayor had announced that the result would not be declared before half-post nine, but it was more than an hour after that time-10 39 p.m.—before the intelligence was displayed in a transparency box from the Mechanics' Institution. JOHN SLAGG, 39, Hertford-street, London, mer- chant and bleacher JOHN ORMEROD SCARLETT THURSBY, Bank Hall, Burnley, Esq.
Majority for Mr. Slagg 545

The scene at the Bull Hotel, whither Mr. Thursby, accompanied by Colonel Thursby, the high sheriff elect. Mr. .1. Greenwood, J.P:, Ald. Baron, and other supporters, wended after the declaration of the poll, was an almost indearibable one. About two hours' previously heavy bets had been made on Mr. Thursby's chances, con- sequently the result came like a thunderclap. Almost perfect silence reigned, being broken only at brief inter- vals by such exclamations as "1 could not have thought it," "The Unionists have sold us," "We'll have Sir George Ttevelyan to fight for us next time," and others dila similar character. In reply to a query as to his condi- tion of mind, a leading town councillor replied." Oh, I feel sick," and immediately paid over the penalty of a rash bet, Alderman Baron tried to suppress his uncomfortable feelings by expressing his surprise at the result, and Colonel Thursby gave vent to similar feelings. The defeated candidate appeared to be on the point of pliy-. sical exhaustion, and very wisely he declined to address the large crowd that collected beneath the window, but lie simply bowed his acknowledgment in reply to a few encouraging cheers. On all hands surprise and dismay were deeply written, and many of the Conservatives and Unionists were heartily glad when the crowd partially dispersed and allowed them to reach their homes unob- served. 'lt is stated that a band had been retained to escort Mr. Thursby to a few places in the town to the inspiring strains of "See, the conquering hero," &c., but the result struck all the music out of their souls, and the bandsmen quietly dispersed, after making laudable efforts to conceal their instruments. The result was received with tremendous enthusiasm. Manchester-road was blocked with thousands of excited people. Immediately after the figures were declared a movement was made in the direction of the Thorn Hotel, the headquarters of Mr. Slagg, where the greatest excitement prevailed. Mr. Slagg was literally besieged with persons who proved the intensity of their feelings by demonstrative shaking of hands all round before the figures were announced. The bearer of the joyful tid- ipza was Mr. W. Collinge, J.P., whose voice was drowned with cheers. After Mr. and Mrs. Slagg had stood at the open window for some time waving their hands, Mr. STAGG, M.P., said: Electors of the borough of Burn- thank you for the magnificent way in which you have done your duty. (Cheers.) You have shown the country that the voice of a great and enlightened con- stituency can give its approval of the policy of a states- man who has provided such abundant benefits for his country. You have ratified the message of peace and good-will that he has sent to suffering ..Ireland. You have made the path of duty easy for others to follow, and you have the honour to lead the van in the forward march towards justice and liberty. My own share in this magnificent fight has been but small. To you Is the honour of victory, for it has been gained by a mighty army of the people. I thank you in the name of the Liberal party for whit you have done to-day. I thank you in the name of down-trodden Ireland. I thank you in my own name, and in that th my wife, who has beellay my side in every stage of this contest, for the honour you have conferred upon me to-day. I now regard myself not only as the Liberal member for Burn- ley, but as the member for every elector.--Unionist, Conservative, or Liberal—ready to do my duty in your service to reward you by faithful acts for the honour you have conferred upon me this day. (Loud cheers.) Alderman JAMES GREENWOOD, who next spoke, said he felt that that was indeed one of the proudest moments of his life. Burnley had decided that it was determined to continue a Liberal constituency. Already a telegram had been sent to the Grand Old Man telling him that Burnley had done its duty, and was in sympathy with his message of peace that he wished to send to the sister

Mr. T. P. O'Coniou, M.P., said : In the name of every Irishman throughout the wide world I say, "God bless Burnley." I can say with perfect truth that you have made the name of Burnley a name of. hope and a word of praise to every lover of liberty, and justice, and peace towards Ireland. You have to-night done honour to the English name and the English nation; for by your vote you have helped to remove the one blot upon the glorious escutcheon of British honour. And you have done honour to the great principles of democracy, because YOU have proved that no appeal to the wisdom, to the knowledge, and above all to the hearts of the masses of the people, will ever be made in vain. You have struck a blow for the union between England and Ire- Ind, because you have proved to the people of Ireland that the people of England wish them well—that the people of England feel generous sorrow for the miseries of Ireland, and bitter hatredlor the wrongs inflicted by Tories and landlords in Ireland.

- _ SHOCKING DiscovEny.—A painful and revolting inci- dent was brought under the notice of the Bristol police on Saturday night. The landlady of a lodging-house in St. Jude's, one of the lowest quarters of the city, found a woman named Lyons lying dead on the floor of a room which she had rented for some weeks. In the apart- ment were her two children, who had remained for 30 hours with the corpse. They were ravenously hungry when discovered, and eagerly devoured the food set before them. The woman died on Friday afternoon while in the act of writing letter appealing to a man for assistance.

SHOCKING SUICIDE IN BOLTON.—On Monday shortly after six a.m., a man named James Ogden, over- looker in the cardroom of Messrs. James Marsden and Sons' cotton spinning mills, Bolton, was found dead in his residence, No. 61, Coe-street, having committed suicide by hanging himself to a book in the wall over the sofa. He had been drinking during Sunday afternoon, but was with his wife at a small festive party at a beerhouse near his house at night. He went home before his wife, locked himself up in his residence, and then committed the rash act.. On his wife returning home she was unable to procure admis- sion, and remained at a neighbour's house all night. On an entrance being forced into the house on Monday morning his.dead body was found. •

WORD Costrwrirrom.—At Clerkenwell County Court. on Monday, before Judge. Eddis a clerk, named Villiers Onunhead, sued the proprietors of a London weekly paper, for £25, which he claimed as first prize in a word competition. Counsel for the plaintiff was pro- ceeding to show that, his client had given in a greater number of English words than had the prize winner, when the judge said it was a curious thing to ask him to decide what was and what was not an Eng4ish word, and he refused to hear the case. The parties might go to the House of Lords if they liked. People who entered such competitions had the right to know Who was to adjudicate before entering, hut if they failed to do so they must abide by the result. He therefore non-suited the plaintiff, with costs.

M. GLADSTONTIAND GENERA!: GORLON'S DEATIL—On Sunday, the 13th inst., the Rev. H. R. Ilaweis, in the course of a sermon on General Gordon at St. James's Church, Marylebone, said—" The first Minister of the Government, Mr. Gladstone, marked his sense of the terrible event by going to see a comic opera on the night that the news. reached London, which sent a thrill of horror through the nation." Mr. William H. Brown, cif Walterton-road, wrote to Mr. Gladstone on the subject, and received the following reply:—" I thank you for your letter, which I have read with regret. The state- ment imputed—l hope in error—to the Rev. Mr. Haweis is simply false. It was the night before the news of General Gordon's death when I kept an'engagetrient to some friends who had kindly invited me to go to the play.—Your faithful and obedient servant, W. E. GLAD- STONE."

IMPORTATION or HORSES.—The importation of horses from Canada for the use of the army is causing some excitement amongst the farmers of the United Kingdom. A question was asked in the House of Commons on Monday, and the answer was to the effect that, although purchases of Canadian horses had taken place, the Go- vernment were desirous of giving every facility to British farmers. The fact is that there is some difficulty in obtaining a full supply of horses suitable for the cavalry and artillery, and for £45, the Government ;price (at least it was the price a short time since), some very questionable animals are added to the army. The Canadian horses which have been distributed amongst the regiments of cavalry and batteries of artillery in England have, writes a London corespondent, turned out remarkably well, and are spoken of in terms of the highest praise by these who have charge of. them. Our farmers cannot expect Canada to neglect the opportunity of legitimate trade in this line of business. , REDUCTION or RAILWAY Rstv.s.—The directors of the Cotton Waste Dealers' Association for some time have had Ander their consideration the railway rates for the carriage of cotton waste, and after frequent interviews and communications with the various railway com- panies, a communication was read at their last regular meeting, held in Manchester, announcing that on and after March Ist a reduced and revised list of rates will come into force, and in future they, will be one standard rate for all classes of cotton waste when sent in full loads of two tons and upwards. This alteration will come as a boon in the present depressed state of the trade, and especially considering the keen competition' and low prices now ruling. The Cotton Waste Dealers Association, consisting of the principal dealers in the trade, which is a very important and extensive one, having connections all over the world, was formed some little time ago to watch over the interests of the mem- bers, and is doing a quiet andsuseful work. The thanks of the association have been tendered to the goods managers of the railway companies for the assistance they have given them, and for their courtesy in melting them to discuss matters iticonnection with trade.
