div.p: FELONIES AT WARRINGTON.

STEALING A £5 NOTE. At an Occasional Court, held on Saturday morn- ing, at the office of Mr. H. B. White, one of the clerks to the county magistrates, a girl named I Elizabeth Naylor, a domestic servant, was charged with stealing a £5 note, the property of William Illampson, a 'mar, on the 11th inst. On that day I Hampson went to lodge at 251, Winwick-road, with a man named Little, by whom prisoner was em- ployed as a servant. Prosecutor had two £5 notes and other money in his possession, and in the pre- sence of the prisoner he wrapped the notes and money in a pocket handkerchief, which he placed In his overcoat pocket. At about nine o'clock he and Mr. Little went to bed and slept together, Hampson placing the coat on the bed. Next morn- ing he missed one of the notes, and accused his bedfellow of having taken it. Little denied the accusation, and subsequently suspicion fell on the prisoner, who, it was learned, had changed a £5 note at the shop of Henry Williamson, grocer and beerseller, 269, Winwick-road. Information was thereupon given to the police, and Sergeant Barnes apprehended and charged prisoner. In reply, she I said "I did not steal it; he gave it to me, and I I changed it at Willis.mson's. I put £3 in my clog, and I lost it; the other I spent,' Prosecutor denied inaving given her any money. Prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Ses- sions. HUNGER AND THEFT. At the Borough Court, on Monday. Gilbert War- burton (17), who lives with his mother at 3, Mor- ris's-tourt, was charged with breaking into the slaughter-house of Frederick Simpson, butcher, in Morris's-yard, between Saturday evening and Sun- day morning, and stealing about 30Ibs. of potatoes, two bags, and a saw, value Bs. Prosecutor, who lives in Wellington-street, saw his slaughter-house ,safe locked up on Saturday evening, and next day it was discovered that it had been broken into. Suspicion fellonprisoner„who admitted having sto- lenthe potatoes,sayingthat he was hungryand took slime home and cooked them. The family to which prisoner belongs were said to be very poor, but it was mentioned by Chief Constable Hunt, that he 'spent fifteenpenee every week in tobacco. Prisoner I had previously been before the magistrates on I a similar charge. He was sent to prison for seven days.

div.head: FOWL STEALING.
div.p: FOWL STEALING.

William Jarvis (20), a single man, and John Tay- lor, a married man, file cutter, 15, Gas-street, were charged with stealing two live hens, Value 68, the property of Thomas Barber, night watchman at the Bank Quay Galvanising Works, who lives at 1, Old Barracks, Bank Quay. Taylor was'also charged with receiving the hens knowing them to have been sto- len, Prosecutor saw his poultry safe on Saturday afternoon, and missed two hens on Sunday morning. Suspicion was directell to Jarvis, who also lives at the Old Barracks, and who keeps company with Taylor's sister. Prisoner was apprehended at Tay- lor's house, where two fowls, partly cooked, were found. When charged Jarvis admitted his guilt, but Tayloi said that he thought the hens belonged to Jarvis. The Bench believed both men, however, to be guilty, and sent them each to prison for a month.

div.head: 'THEFT OF A BAG OP FLOUR.
div.p: 'THEFT OF A BAG OP FLOUR.

At the Borough Court, on Tuesday morning, a tnan named John Warburton was charged with dealing a bag of flour, value lie, the propertY of John Broadhurst, provision dealer, Winwick-street, between Sunday afternoon and Monday morning, from a bakehouse in Oliver-street. Maria Warbur- ton, his mother, was charged with receiving the flour, knowing it to have been stolen. The loss of the bag of flour, which had been placed with others in the bakehouse in Oliver-street, having been no- tified to the police. inquiries were made which led to the police visiting the house where prisoner lives. He was in bed, and in the room was the bag of flour. His mother was baking cakes downstairs, apparently with the flour that had been stolen. The male prisoner was found• guilty, and was sent to prison for three months, and the female was dis- charged. Arnfr

WARRINGTON UNION —WORKHOUSE MASTER A.ND MATSON WANTED.—The Guardians of this Union will, at their Meeting. to be heid on the 16th day of March, 1887, at the Board-room, in Warr ington, at k leven o'cicck, proceed to the ELECTION of a Master and Matron for the Workhouse. The salary of the Master will be £BO per annum, and the salary of the Matron will be £4l per annum, both with the usual rations, washing, and furnished apart- ments. The candidates must be husband and wife, and they must not be over 45 nor under 30 years of she. Testimon als as to sharacter. sobriety, and competency to discharge the duties prescribed by the orders of the Local Government Board, will be required. Applications to be Sited up in the handwrit- ing of the parties applying, stating the particulars set forth, In a form to ba obtained at toy office cia personal or written re- quest, must be forwarded to me post free, on or buf ore Thurs. oay, the 10th day of Mara), 1887, endorsed "Application for the situations of Workhouse Master and Matron.' The person appointed Master will be required to give security, with two sureties, or a guarantee. society, in the sum of £lOO, for the due performance of his duties. Candidates are not to attend un'ese written .to for that pur- pose. Canvassing the Guardians Is strictly prohibited, and will constitute a disquadfication. (By order) J. O. BtiTT'3lC, Bewsey Chambers, Clerk to tha Guardians. Warrington, February 13. 1831.

WELLINGTON COLLEGE, WELLINGTON, SHROP- SHIRE. These new and extensive builtlings. com- manding a beautiful view of the surrounding country, are splendidly situated, and have been specially built for Educa- tional Purposes. Football and cricket fields, gymnasium, and four tennis lawns. Preparations for the Universities, Profes- sions, or Business. In the College of Preceptors' Examination, 1884, the First Place in England was won in Drawing, and in the Cambridge Junior the Second Place in England in Scrip- ture. At Christmas, 1885, the Second Place In the First Class was won, and the same boy gained more Special Certificates than any other candidate in England, and also won the Second Prize offered by :he College of Preceptors for General Pro- ficiency. Seven boys paihsed the Cambridge, Two Seniors and Five Juniors, two of thelffx gaining honours. Five boys passed the London University Examination last June, one being 49th In honours, and the others winning places in the First Divi- sion. More thara 100 boys have passed these Examinations during the past three years. There roe 80 pupils under a most Efficient Staff of Resident Masters. The Ooliege is now being enlarged, and by Christmas there will be accommodation for 30 additional boarders. Prospectus and further information on application to Mr. 7. BAYLEY, the erincipal. _ -

THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 16, 1887.

IT has been a matter of rejoicing every- where, to Liberals who do not call themselves Liberal Unionists, that a Liberal has been returned for Burnley by such a large majority. It was confidently expected by the leading Liberals of the borough that Arr. ':LAGG would be returned, but it was not expected that he would have a majority of 545. The Tories, too, were confident; the result of their canvass was most promising, and that they had good cause for being hopeful is shown by the fact that their candidate, Mr. THURSBY, polled 172 votes more than were given for Mr. RYLANDS last year. Mr. RYLANDS, in 1886, had a majority of 43 with 4,209 ; Mr. THUltssY is in a minority of 545, although as many as .4481 electors recorded their votes in his favour. Both sides worked exceedingly hard—it is questionable if a con- stituency of ro,ooo voters was ever before so closely polled—and it has thus happened that the Tory candidate is a long way be- hind whilst securing what he thought would be a winning total. The chief cause for re- joicing is in the factlthat the election affords reliable evidence that but few Liberal Unionists can be brought to take Lord HAR- TINGToN's advice to vote Toiy rather than vote for a Home Rule candidate' and, fur- ther, that the bulx of the Liberal Unionists are showing themselves disposed to accept the inevitable. We say the bulk—we cannot say all—for it is not to be denied that the majority for Mr. SLAGG is not so large as it would have been if the Liberal party had been a thoroughly united party. It should be remembered that in 1•835 Mr. RYLANDS had a majority of '667. There was no split then, so far as the Unionists were concerned; but there was a split as to the Irish vote. The Irish were advised to vote Tory at this election in Burnley, as elsewhere, and there can be no question that, large as was Mr. RYLANDS' majority on this occasion, it was considerably reduced by Mr. PARNELL'S manifesto. We mention these facts not by way of minimising "a famous victory," but in order that our Liberal readers may realise that the breach with the Liberal Unionists is but half closed, and that they must con- tinue to work until it is wholly closed. IThere is a disposition to turn round on Lord HARTINGTON in this hour of triumph ' and ostracise him. But Liberals must show themselves liberal-minded ; the party that advocates toleration must be tolerant. Gran- ted that it is galling to have a (leader in the Liberal ranks appealing to Liberals to vote Tory ; but if he honestly thinks that, at this juncture of affairs, opposition to Home Rule ahould over-ride emery other consideration, what else can he do ? It may he said that he can stand aside, or "go over;" like Mr. GOSCHEN ; but that is a matter which he mist settle with his own conscience, and so long as Lord HARTINGTON acts conscien- tiously he ought, even apart from considera- tiOn for his services in the past, to be treated with respect. And, to take lower ground, to consider the question solely as one of expe- diency, we hold that it is unwise to go out of the s'ay to alienate the Liberal Unionists. Burnley is not as other boroughs are,; it is in the proud position of having invariably returned a Liberal to Parliament; and its Liberal margin is so large that, as events show, when it is a case of opposing a'Tory pure and simple he has no chance, irrespec- tive of difficulties either as to the Irish on the one hand, or the Liberal Unionist on the other. This, we need hardly say, cannot be said of many other Lancashire constituencies. Warrington, St. Helens, and 'Widnes may be regarded as Liberal ; but the opposing force is so strong—the numbers are so nearly bal- anced—that there is no room for the loss of a detachment either of Nationalists at one elec- tion, or of Liberal Unionists at another. With regard to the latter class of politi- cians, as they have not presented them- selves in each constituency as an organised body, their numerical strength has, as a rule, been under-rated ; but no one can study the retnrns of the last General Election without realising that the Liberal party need not expect to come into power with a work- ing majority, except by the aid of the votes of the Liberal Unionists. It is because we perceive this, and because we perceive, too, that Liberal Unionists are tired of holding aloof, that we would seek to win them back rather than drive them from the ranks. Let it be ever borne in mind that Concilia- tion rather than Coercion may be good for
Liberal Unionists as well as for Irish Na- tionalists.

THE HOME SECRETARY has been talking !in a general sort of way about the views of the Government.on the Irish land question. llt will, we imagine, be startling to most of the old-fashioned Tories, and some of the new-fashioned Radicals, to find that Mr. MATTHEws shows himself as liberal as Mr. GLADSTONE without showing himself as con- servative ; he goes quite as far in disposing of I Irish landlords; but he does not, as Nlr. I GLADSTONE did, show how he is going to I give security to the British taxpayer for the money that is to be advanced. Speaking at Birmingham, on Tuesday, he said : They all know there was an agrarian question, which never would be solved unless they succeeded in transferring the ownership of the land from those , who now possessed it to those who were tilling the soil. That such a thing was possible no one who , had studied politics could doubt. It had been done in Prussia, Austria, Bavaria, and even Russia. It had been found possible on the Continent to pay the landlords with debentures representing the value of their land. These bore interest, payable by the occupier, representing not only remuneration for the use of the capital, but also a sinking fund by which that capital was gradually, and in the course of years, paid off. These debentures he knew passed from hard to hand in Bavaria, and were a favourite investment for the savings of the working classes. The whole operation worked with perfect smooth- nets. It was true that the operation would not succeed unless they had the ultimate security of the State. 11 ithout State guarantee and management it would not work, but he believed in Ireland it would be pb.-sible to use British credit without its costing a single penny to the British taxpayer. It is a pity he did not proceed to explain how he means to give a " State guarantee," and "use British credit without its costing a single penny to the British taxpayer." This is, of course, what Mr. GLADSTONE proposed I to do • and he went on to demonstrate how it could be done. Under the provision of the Irish ' Land Bill, it was intended to advance the sum of L 50,000,000 for the purchase of tenants' I holdings in Ireland. This at four per cent. I meant £2,000,000 per year; and the British taxpayer grew alarmed as to the payment of ! this sum. It was urged that, if Irish tenants I would not pay their landlords, they would not pay the interest on the Fifty Millions, and that the money would be lost. There were few, as it seemed to us, who took the ! ! trouble to glance at the security which Mr. I GLADSTONE provided for the payment of the interest; and in view of what is now under consideration by the present Government it may be as well to revert to this feature of the bill. Speaking broadly, then, Mr. GLAD- STONE proposed to !take control of Irish revenues from Customs and Excise, &c., and out of these, as a first charge, to meet the claim for the Imperial contribution, the charge for the constabulary, and the ' Lz,ooo,ooe for interest on the money ad- vanced. In his speech in the House of Com- mons, on !introducing the bill, he said— "We want to get £6,242,000, and that is secured upon -X, r 0,850,000, no portion of wtlich can be applied for any other purpose until our claim in respect of the £6,242,000 is satisf.ed:" From this it will be seen that ! there was a margin of over four millions inl hand by way of security for the two millions of interest. But politicians were too excited last year to work these little sums in arith- metic; and the result was that the Land Bill was howled down by those who knew least about it. The Tory Government are about to ! try what they can do in the same direction ; and they must be watched. There may be a , very wide and wholly unsatisfactory margin between promise and performance.

SCARCELY a week passes without someone being maimed or killed through people meddling with loaded firearms. In this dis- trict there have .been two such acdents within forty-eight hours of each other. On Friday a young man named JENKINsow, liv- ing at Lowton, took up a gun, which, he I chought, was unloaded; but he furnished it with a can, pulled the trigger, shot his sister in the head, and killed her. On Saturday, at Warrington, a lad named Isxnawooni was playing with two schoolfellows in a store-' room in Bewsey-street, when one of them, named WAGGTAFFE, picked up a pistol. Whilst he was examining it, it went off; the shot struck ISHERWOOD on the forehead.; he was badly injured, and narrowly escaped with his life. The first thought that strikes one on hearing the particulars of these and other cases is that great carelessness is exhibited on the part of the owners of.srearms. It ought not to have been possible for the lad, or the young man, to pick up a loaded weapon with- out knowing that it was loaded. People who load guns or pistols should have them under lock and key;, and they ought to be tnade to feel that they are in some degree 're- spon-sible if they leave these deadly play- things "lying about." The evidence given at the inquest, on Monday, on the body of the unfortunate young woman shows that the gun had been kept in a corner of the kitchen. It had remained there loaded for eight or nine months, although the young man who lived 'in the house, and who handled it with such fatal effect on Friday, was unaware that it was loatfed. He took it up, and he put on a badly fitting ,cap, and it was whilst he was experimenting with this cap that the gun went off and the sister was killed. It is a common story—a case of playing with loaded firearms, and the most lamentable feature is that it is so common. It seems to be a mat-, ter of course for a boy or young rnan to take up a pistol or gun when opportunity offers, and, as it is equally a inatter of cotrse to as- sume that 'the weapon is unloaded, the ques- tion arises whether it would not heclesirable to visit the person with a penalty who leaves loaded firearms in accessible places. It is true that a•gun will do no harm if left alone; but the same may be said of revolving ma- chinery; and yet the Legislature has deemed it necessary, for the protection of life and limb, to insist that certain portions of ma- chinery shall he fenced off. Loaded firearms are quite as dangerous as revolving wheels, and they, too, require, in some way or other, to be "fenced .off."

TITHE RENT REDUCTION IN CHESLIIRE.—The Hon. , Howard Vyse, who .owns the tithes ovdr a consider- able area near Tarvin, Cheshire, has intimated to the tenantry his intention of returning them 10 per lcent on the amounts due. This is the second year in succession that the Hon. Howard Vyse has re- turned his tenantry 10 per cent on the tithes. THE LATE Mn. P. RY,LANDS, ALP.,, AND Mn. C. BnoenßENT.—Atthe Dareibury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, the Chairman (Mr, E. Greenell) referred to the deaths of the late Mr. P. Rylands, M.P., and Mr. C. Broadbent. He said that since the last sitting of. the court they had been deprived by death of two of the magistrates of that division, Sir. Rylands and Mr. Broadbent, both of whom were highly respected by their brother justices. As regarded Mr. Rylands, his Parliamentary duties had prevented his fre- quent attendance at the court, but Mr. Broadbent had been most assiduous in his attendance, and by his remarkable kindliness and courtesy of disposi- tion and attention to business had won the respect and admiration of those who' sat with him. "TOUCH AND GO."
"Truth" says :—The " fi st class" Minis• terial pension (le. £2,,000 a year) which fell in by the death of Lord Iddesleigh, has been booked by Lord Cross.

"A doctor living near Margate has married a cook who inherited £6o 000 a few months ago." Perhaps a better • way of putting it would be to say the doctor has married an estate worth £60,000, and taken the cook as part of the live stock.

The Birkenhead Board of Guardians has " achieved greatness " ; it has the reputation of being " the highest Union in England in regard, to the consumption of drink." There are people who, if they cannot b.t famous, will run the risk of becommg in- famous.

The police have been enforcing the law as to lotteries at St. Helens and at Widnes. Having caught the small fry on the market ground, they will, perhaps, take courage, and deal with the leviathan offenders who prac- tice at banal s. There ought not to he any ground for the suggestion that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor.

Colonel Greenall has a curious way of complimenting the burgesses of Warrington. Speaking at a Smoking Concert over which he presided, he referred to the recent Town's Meeting as a hole-and-corner meeting. Considering that it was called by the Deputy- Mayor, that it was publicly advertised, hell in a public hall, and was well attended by the public, the description is as absurd as it is derogatory. Where has the Colonel been ? His wits seem to have been wool-gathering.

He is entitled, of course, to his opinion that freeing the Library would be "a queer way of celebrating Her Majesty's Jubilee." The military man never did care to en- courage reading; he does not get his re- cruits from the reading class. He does not wish to see any permanent benefit from the Jubilee ; he prefers something that begtns and ends—in smoke.

The Bishop of Peterborough has been de- nouncing those "mothers who received into their houses and, worse still, gave the hands of their daughters in matrimony to men who had caused and created these victims of fal- len humanity, as a peer's robe, like charity, was supposed by women to hide a multitude of sins." This protest might have come earlier; but, " better late than never."

It is to be feared that the clergy are dumb on tkese social questions because they have "great expectations" from rich men. Dukes and lords have 'good livings" to dispose of, so, although their own lives may be anything but good, not a word must be said which would give offence. There is a holy horror, of-course, at the prevailing drunkenness; but so tong as the flourishing brewer contributes to school funds'and church building, we must not have so much as a whisper against " the trade." As Byron has it—
"Oh for a-forty-parson power to chant Thy praise, Hypocrisy!

It is not pleasant to be summoned before the magistrates ; and it is not pleasant, either, to be jostled in Sankey-street by " fellow- lads," who resort to this practico as a means of working off their super-abandant energy. Let "the boys" think of these two things as connected with each other, and behave better for the future. It may not always be a case of , being" let off "as,on Monday, on payment of costs, and being bound over.

The two Italian fasting men who thought to make money out of an exhibition of starvation have missed their way. They are now so poor that there is danger of their starving for a somewhat longer period than that which they prescribed for themselves. Fasting doesn't pay; it would be in every 'Rey better to try a vFeasting exhibition; for if there happened to be a financial loss, there would probably be:a set-off in the way of a physical gain.

General Gorldon seems to have been much impressed with the lack of resolute aim in politicians. Ina letter which has just been published, addressed to "a young member of Parliament," he says :--",770u must know that as a rule our Ministers are a hand-to- mouth set. Enough for the day its evil' is their maxim.' They have a lack-lustre eye 'for ,anyttling which does not precs. They lake not any opposition. They are much clerk and official ridden." This is -very pertinent. and, as to style, it ,might be an extract (rota Carlyle. •

lit =must be very gratifyinE to Mr. Ellis Lever to have had Mr. Gladstoce's congratu- lations on the " great work" which he hes done in fighting the battle of purity in the transaction of Corporate business. Mere ' are so many "wheels within wheels," E.nd these wheels have go much acower to crus4, that he must be a brave man with a long, purse vim will risk their sharp ;teeth'. Mr. ,Lever has done all this, and has come out :unscathed. The exposure of rottenness offends one's nostrils; , but when,it is removed The air is the sweeter.

Shadesof Wordsworth, Southey, and Cnie—kl ridge—it tis proposed to carry a railway toti Arnbleside.! Could desecration farther goi The charm of the Lake District, in addition to its unrivalled natural beauty, is in its sense:l of remoteness from the fever and the fret of our work-a-day life. Wordsworth speaks of "a lamb Zeft somewhere all alone—the plaintive spirit of the,colitude." But no more of this, after the shrieking demon of a railway loco- motive makes an appearance. Our best wish for the promoters of this -scheme is that it will fail ; they know not whet they do. The Commissioners of Northern Lighthouses dined together in Edinburgh, at the public expense, on the ,rsth January, 1886. Forty- seven neraons sat down to dinner, and the bill came to £579 as, This is nearly £4 per head, the item for wine, being at 'the rate of .£a 65 8d per head. ,General Neal Dow once said the English were the most drunken people under the face of heaveo. Could he have been hearing of the way these Commissioners dine ? We don't :mow what is to be done in the matter ; perhaps the Commissioners will be surcharged they ought to be discharged. --- Canon Lefroy, the new Archdeacon of War- rington, spoke at St. Barnabas' tea meeting, on Tuesday evening, and, in the course of his remarks, urged the necessity of enlarging the day schools. In doing so he took occasion to suggest that, if they did not take that course they might have a School Board rate to pay of is. 6d. in the pound. An Arch- deacon ought to know better than talk non- sense of this kind. The average rate for the whole of England is less than sevenpence in the

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT Of the value of eyesight. In many instances when they krst find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- tacles which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Franks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, Manchester, and 143, Lord-street, Southport, has invented his" Perfection " Spectacles, which he adopts at either of the above addresses at 7$ 61 per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to be equalled in the country for clearness. coolness, aryl rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight " tree on apolication.—Adrt. WIDNES WLLSII WESLEYAN CHIPEL.—Mr. Barnett Dut- ton on Monday afterno in offered for sale the Welsh Wes- Ityan Chapel, shuated in Croinwell-street, but as the reserve price was not reached the property was Withdrawn. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.— Mr. J Crlover delivered an interesting. lecture on " Combus- tion," illustrated by experiments, to the mernbera of this class on Wednesday evening, and at the conclusion be was heartily thanked.

r/lIMITIVE METHODISM AT IVIDNES —During the past wPek special evangelistic services have been conducted bv Mr. W. Tharme, of Liverpool, in Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel, Widnes. They commenced on Sunday, when two services were held, and a service has been held each evening since. Each service has been fairly well attended.

LECTURE AT RUNCORN.—On Monday evening the Rev. W. W. Preston, M.A., delivered a lecture entitled " A trip to Rome," to a good audience, in Trinity Schoolroom. Mr. W. Hankinson occupied the chair. Tne lecture was illus- trated by excellent dissolving views from a powerful magic lantern, which was manipulated by Mr. James Frith. The proceeds ware to be devoted to the Mill Brow Ragged School. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—At a spacial meeting of the Widnes Local Board, on Thursday, the chairman (Mr. F. H. Gossage) remarked that as he would be ineligible for the position of returning officer at the next election, it was necessary that the Board should appoint another gentleman to perform the duties of that office. On the motion of Mr. F. Heyee, seconded by Mr. J. Taylor, it was unanimously decided that Dr. O'Keeffe be the returning officer. WIDNES TRISH NATIONALISTS.—IR connection with the Widues branch of the Irish Na-ional League an entertain- mPur was given in the League Hall, Sr. Paul's Buildings, on Tuesday evening. Dr. O'Keeffa presided, and there was an excellent attendance. Songs, Ac., were contributed by Messrs. Williamson (Runcern), Kiddie, Singleton, Stones, and Starkey •, Mrs. Horan and Miss Edwards. Mr. Moore O'Farrell delivered an eloquent address on Irish sub. jects. WESTON WESLE CAN Scuoote—A lecture was delivered in this 'reboot on Wednesday evening, by the Rev. A. I'. Wat- son., eutitled " William Carey, the Consecrated Cobbler," Mr. T. Leach, jun., of Runcorn, presided. The lecture was attentively listened to by a large and appreciative audience, who frequently applauded the lecturer's remarks. Messrs. Kirkham and Jelin Ball moved and seconded a vote of thanks to the lecturer, and a vote of thanks to the chairman con- cluded the proceedings. FIRE AT WIDSES —OR Tuesday evening the office of Messrs. Potts and Appleton, coal agents, Lugsdale was conaumed by fire. The structure was of wood, and when the fire was discovered there was no hope of arreeting tbe flames, as there was no water at band, and therefore no attempt was made to extinguish them. The damage is es- timated at £5O. as all the books and papers were destroyed. The stove that was fixed in the place is considered to be the cause of the conflagration. GOOD TEXPLARY AT KUNCORN —ln connection with the Prosperity of Runcorn Lodge 1.0.G.F., an " open " meeting was held on Wednesday eveniug, when there was a fair at- tendance of members and friends. Brother J Faulkner, W.C.T., occupied the chair. A very pleasant evening was spent. The choir recently formed, under the conductorship of Mr. 1. Fox, contributed several part songs, and a pro- gramme of songs, recitatioes, Arc., was gone through by Sisters Woodward•and Foster, and Brothers T. Wilson, J. Faulkner, S. Ing,lesfield, and E. Davies, with Messrs. A. Bibby and F. Eden.

FAITTURE OF A RUNCORN SIIIP CRANDLER.—A rnsetiraz of the creditors of Mr. W. T. Shore, ship chandler, Alex- andra Buildings, Top Locks, Runcorn, was held on Tuesday at Liverpool. The statement of accounts presented by Mr. J. W. Lightburn, chartered accountant, showed that the liabilities of the debtor amounted to upwards of £2,000. Mr. Shore offered a composition of 5s in the pound, but in consequence of the oppesiticn of one or two creditors no arrangement could be entered into, and -en Wednesday the debtor filed his petition. Mr. Lightburn was appointed by the'Court to prepare a statement of accounts.

. . PNTATION TO A FOOTBALL PLATER AT RUNCOR!..T.— There was a large gathering of persons interested in football at the café of Mr. Arthur Riley, on Friday evening, when the members of the Recreation Football Club presented W. Faulkner with a handsome cap in commemoration of his *election to play for the Cheshire Comity against Yorkshire. Faulkner was formerly a sub•captain of the Recreation Club, and in tesponding to the g ft, which was presented by Mr. T. Whinyrtes, he said th at thougil now a member of-the Runcorn club, he should ever regard with pleasure the experience he gained while with the Recreltion. RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA NOUSE CO., LIMICE.D.— The ninth annual meeting of the shareholders of this c4lO- - was held on Monday evening, at the company's pre- mises, High-street. Mr 0 Jackson presided. The report of the directors atated the the receipts from refreshments amounted to £982 Os 33, and the nett profits to £1.16 15s lid. It was recommended that flve per cent should be paid on the paid up capital, and the earn of £BB 15s Id carried to the reserve fund. The report was adopted on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr John Simpson. and it was decided that the recommended percentage should be paid on the proposition of Mr P Speakman, seconded Iv Mr R Norman. Messrs -liackson and Speakman were enanim- ousiy re-elected directors.

CATuoLie BALL AT Win.—The nineteenth annual ball, arranged by the Catholics of Widnes, took place in the Volunteer Hall on Monday evening, and was attended with the abundant success enat has.characterised similar gather- ings in the past. The arrangements had been admirably carried out by a cominbtee, of which Mr. S. Quinn was the bon..cec., and the co wfart end convenience of tire visitors, who numbered 200, had been thoroughly consulted. By a judicious display of bunting and banners, and the adorn- ment-afforded by the landscape drawings of Mr. Kiddie. the room was given a bright and attractive appearance. Danc- ing was commenced at nine o'clock, and continued until four o'clock, to the strains of Mr_ Gordon's quadrille b•oni. Mr. Tallon, jun., and Tr.r. Carroll ably officiated as M.C's. The refreshments were provided by Mr. Gerrard, of the Alexandra Hotel.

A IkCHELORe TE..t.PaRT7 WlDNES.—Whatia known I as " The Annual Bachelor's Tea Party" took place on Shrove Tuesday, in the Primitive Nlethodist Chapel, Simms' Cross. The meeting derives its name from the fact that the tea and subsequent entertainment are entirely provided end. sustained by the male 'members of the congregation, the fair sex havizg nothing whatever to do with theta ex.c.pt par.' ticipate in the enjoyment. About '2OO persons sat down to tea, the, following gentlemen presiding at the tables : Messrs. Collason, Owens, Adams, Rees, Crosby, Jones," Ricbarda, Elewson, and Smith. -Subsequently an entertain- ment was-given, under the presidency of Mr T D Peters. The programme consisted of glees, ronnds, songs, and read- ings, and was sustained in a very able manner bythe fol- lowing :--Cessra Rees, Drought, Hewson, Lee, Rellason, A, Calvert, mild G flnime, and Masters Bate and P During an 4aterval in the .programme, an eloquent address was given ley Mr W Tharrne, of Liverpool. At the close of the proceedings a vote of thanks Wa3 accorded the chairman, land to all those who had been in any way connected with ; the entertainment.

LAcßosne—Widnes a. Fairfietd: This match was tialayed at Hough Green on Baturday, and resulted in & vic- tory for the home team by e 4 goals toil. Both sides were well represented, but good play was out of the question. owing to the 'lumpy state of the ground. Widnes lest the Pees, and therhad to play against the wind and a strong -sun. Fairfield were the first to score, by a scrimmage, %tar Vctster equalised almost itnmediatelv. After some ecual play, G lialealtscored another goal for Widnes, but Fair- field playing upetrongly soon made it two all. At half- time the score was Widnes 3, Fairfield 2. Soon after half- time Wilsoa scored for Widnes, and Fairfiekl made desperate efforts to pull the match out of the fire, but only succeeded iii adding one mosepoint. Ihe hone teanyhad just pat the bail through for the fifth time ,when time 'WAG called, leaving Widnes winners as above. For Fairfield. Presely and Canahonme played beet; but Widnes, having had ..no match for 'the last four weeks, played badly. Forster, R H Gossage, and R Halsall being the only ones to allow op in anything like their true form. BE White made a very creditable first appearance in .goal for the winners. WIDNZS FREE LIBRARY CoanerrmEno—A meeting of this I committee was held on Wednesday at Alforde 'Chambers. Mr. H. W. Deacon presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. J. Morrisoo, and Mr. J. T. Atieni clerk to the Local Board. A letter was read from Mt R. Lewis, who I announced kis resignation as a member of the Committee. It must, be added, have escaped the notice of the Board when they asked him to accept the seat that he was a resident of Ditton and not in his own parson a ratepayer of Widnes. From the action Of the committee he had tome to the conclusion that the above facts were not consonant with his retaining his place, and by making way for a Widnes ratepayer he thought he was adopting the best course.—The Chairman remarked that this was a matter for the Local Government I Board to deal with, and not the Committee.—The tender ef Messrs. Hough and Company for the supply of newspapers, periodicals, and magazines to the Free Library was accepted. —The Clerk reported that the Library had received a dona- tion of books on Poetry and fiction, and a number of m a- zines, from the Committee of the Science and Art School. and the cordial thanks of the meeting were accorded to the Committee on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe, seconded by the Chairman.—lt was decided to advertise for an assistant librarian at a salary of 10a per week.

MEMORIAL TO TUE LATE CANON I:lAllEl...LT.—Upwards of £BO has been subscribed towards the fund for placing a mural tablet in the ParislaChurch in memory of the late Canon Barclay, vicar of Runcorn. A considerable sum has also been subscribed towards the completion of the church of St. Michael aad All Angels. ST. Amßaosz Crtuacm, WIDNES.—On Thursday evening a concert was given in Page-lane Mission Room, in aid of the funds of St. Ambrose Church. The room was crowded with an appreciative audience. A cipital entertainment was given by Mr. George Barton's (St. Helens) concert party, whose expenses were generously defrayed by Mr. Valentine, a consistent supporter of St. Ambrose Church.

THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court yesterday, before Mr. A.l homes, John Craig, 48 years of age, was brought up on remand, charged with having attempted to commit suicide on the 18th February, by jumping into the Weaver Canal. The prisoner, who had been confined in Knutsford Gaol for seven days was not considered to be in a fit condition to be liberated and he was remanded to Dutton Workhouse for a fortnight. A DITTON HORSE , SLAUGHTERER IN TROUBLE. At Widnes- Petty Sessions, On Thursday, Joseph Tharme, licensed victualler, Ditton, was charged with having used a horse that had been delivered to him for the purpose of be- ing slaughtered.. The defendant admitted his guilt. There were also two other summonses against the defendant in regard to the same horse and Inspector Wood intimated that if the defendant would pay the costs in all three be would withdraw them. The defendant consented, and paid 303 costs.

A MONTH'S HARD LABOUR FOR CHANGE OF lIESIDIENCE. —Before Mr. A. Thomae and Captain C. W. Haziehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, Thomas Carrington. a man subject to police stipervieion, was ch.rgrd with falling to notify his change of residence to Supt. Hollingworth. On the 31st October the prisoner came to Runcorn and took up his resi. dance in Cholmontieley-place, and duly reported himself to the police. On the 11th December he departed without signifying his intention to the police, and be was apprehen- ded at Chorley in Lancashire. He was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

A Rutrcontt SHIP BROKER AND His DISTRICT RATE. —At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, W. J. Shore, ship broker, rizc, Percival's-lane, was summoned by the Board of Commissioners for the sum of £3 16s 11d, being the amount doe from him on account of the General District Rte Mr. M. Barker, collector, proved the account.—Mr. J. W. Light. burn said he appeared on habil f of the defendant to consent to an order /*mg maie for payment in a fortnight. He had had the management of the defendant's affairs placed in his hands, and.he WAS endeavouring to make an arringe- went with the creditors. If he failed in that endeavour, he should file the debtor's petition. The Bench Made the order for payment. RuNconw GYMNASIUM.—The members of this institution have presented Mr IL J. Fall, of the Liverpool Gymnasium, with a handsome travelling bag .in recognition of his ser- vices as teacher since the establishment of the gymnasium. Mr. Fall has rendered the highest service to the gymnasium under his charge, and it is noteworthy that his assistance was given without fee or reward. He relinquishes his posi- tion through having to leave England to fill an appointment in Brazil: The second round in the Liverpool Olatrict Challenge Shield competition has been fixed to take place on or before March 15th. The team representing the Run- corn Gymnasium, after defeating Widnes, have been drawn against the New Brighton Gymnasium. RUNCORN Fours/at. CLUB —The Runcorn team have a record of successes for the present season that is the envy of the surrounding clubs, and their prowess, coupled with the well-directed exertions of their indefatigable secretary. Mr. J. E. Langshaw, is receiving recognition in quarters where hitherto the club has been practically unknown or ignored. A list is being prepared for next season that will give the utmost satisfaction to the supporters of the team. Dates have already been arranged with the powerful organisations of Swinton, Cardiff, Llanelly, Liverpool. 9alford, Dews- bury, Manningham, Wakefield Trinity, Liverpool Old Boys, Birkenhead Park, and New Brighton; audit is to be hmed the players will prove equal to the great task that is before them next winter. ST. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.—Mr. A. R. Nor- man presided over the monthly meeting, held on Wednes- day night, when a programme of recitations by the ciail- dren,and music by the choir was gone through. A duet WAS given by Misses Thomas and Dobson, and a selo by Mrs. R. Evans. A special feature of the entertainment was a dialo- gue entitled "The flower Queen's court," the rac of the Queen being sustained by Miss Kirkham. The flowers were represented by the Misses Williams, Herron, Jones, Clough, Sherratt, Leyland, E. Kirkham, C. Kirkham, M. Kirkham, and B. M. Clough. The platform was decorated with an arch erected by Mr. Kirkham, and tastefully trimmed with flags, evergreens, and flosers by Mrs. F. Jones, Mrs. R. W. Barron, Miss Jepson, and Miss Kirkham. The dialogue was enhanced by selections of music by Mr. John Evans, who kindly lent his American organ for the occasion. . _

A ittfliCOßN BEERSELLER CONVICTED.—SiraII Littlewood keeper of the Albion Inn, Peel-street, Runcorn, was brought before the Runcorn Magistrates on Monday charged with having on the 14th February (1) kept open her house for the sale of intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours, (2) with stallion. to a drunken person named Thomas Littler, (3) and with selling daring prohibited home to Thomas Littler. Evidence was given by Inspector Millington, P. C. Blair, and P. C. Charles Potts, and it appeared that the house was open at ten minutes past eleven, and the constables going inside, found the womaes husbaed seated at a piano playing. Thomas Littler a atone Mason, was present. He wag drunk and had a glass of porter before him. The defendant de- nied that she had any porter in the house, and said that all Littler had was a bottle of cider. It was contended that Littler was not drunk, and that nothing was served after eleven o'clock. After denat tare at the officers they discov- ered that the clock was wrong. The bench convicted on the firm end second charges and the defendant had to pay a total sum of £2 2a Od.

PRAT a PACKETS AT WIDNES: POLICE PROSECITTION.—A young titan named Patrick Gill, who described himself as a carter from Manchester, was brought before the Widnes magietrates, on Monday, charged with having, on Saturday night, at Widnes Market-place, conducted a lottery. The prisoner's stock•in-trade consisted of a stool, and a box con- taintng prize packets each containing a ring, and occasion- ally a threepenny piece was discovered, to induce the spectators to pay their penny and try their luck. A con- stale who was watching saw the prisoner make up 30 packets, and only placed one threepenny piece in one packet. Shortly afterwards he seized the stock, and took the prisoner into cuetody. It the police station the box was searched, and 29 packets were found. There was not a coin in one of them. In answer to Inspector Wood, the constable said the rirws were worth about a penny a dozen. The prisoner elid he had paid toll for the market kround, and he did not know that lotteries were illegal. Another man had p-evionelv had a similar stall. The Bench im- posed a tine of 10t tml costs,-6s 6J, being a halipenity WIG tkan was found in the prisoner's possession.

ANOTHER VIOLY.NT FOREIGNER AT WIDNES. At WM- nes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. T. S. Mamie, a young man named John Lingas, of Polish nationality, -employed at the Atlas Chemical Works, was brought np on 'remand charged with haying on Sunday night unlawfully wounded a man named Richard Potter, a chemical labourer, • who !iv', at 55, Cromwell-street. it appeared that themes and several ethers •C IMO out of Hunter's public-house, in 'Hutchinson-street. at closing time on Sunday night. Pot- ter obsaryiag that the prisoner had held of his brother went to the rescue \of the latter, whereupon the prisoner struck Potter on thefieft vide of the face and knocked him down. Whilst he was lying on the ground the prisoner kicked tim , savagely on the head severat times, and he cried "murder," but the more be shouted the more the prisoner kicked him. 'Subsequently Mr. ti,oyer, manager at the works of Messrs. Mort. Liddel, and Co. &mod Potter lying on the ground, and assisted hhn to Dr. McCambridge's surgery, where his wounds were dressed. Tie had lost a great quantity of blood, and suffered much pain. Be was confined to bed 'until Wedneadat morning. Dr. McCambridge described 'the wounds on Potter's head and slid they were of a very -dangerous character. Potter was now, hoverer, out of ell danger. The prisoner, who was weeping dar- ing the greater part of the proceedings, denied the -charge entirely, and even went upoct his knees to pro- test his innocence. He was committed to the Quarter Sea- plions for trial.

A RIISCORN Connives Accorsr.—At Runcorn County 'Court, on Tuesday, Messrs. P. Smith and Co., chemists, 'High-street, Runcorn, sued Mr. Robert Gorst. confectioner, 'High-street, Runcorn, for the sum of £5 55 Cl. The bill of .carticulars showed that the charges were principally for operations in dentistry. Mr. Gorst had paid £3 Os ed into mart in settlemnnt of the claim. At the outset his Honour qedgo Wynne Ff.tulkes inquired ef the plaintiff who the "'company" were, and Mr. Smith replied "nobody." He Simply traded under that title. His Honour remarked that as the plaintiff was alone registered as a dentist he must sue in his own name, and he trotsed the "company" from the plaisst. The defendant objected to an item of £1 is for a " regulation case" supplied for the parpoee of straightening his taughter's teeth, alleging that it VR9 obtained from Mr. Fraser, dentist, of Liverpool. and that the price was to be hall a guinea. The plaintiff said Mr. Fraser was a gentle- man who did a little mechanical work for him occasionally, and-the defendant admitted that he haduot paid the account to or-received a bill from Mr. Fraser. The defendant also took exception to two items of 5s for "filing teeth." Mr. Fraser tilled him A moth- on the 10th January, and the composition came out next day, and the tooth wan. filled again on the 24,11. The plaintiff denied this; he did the work trimself.--The defendant: Your Honour, he has never filied me one. Mr. Fraser did them both. He knows it iv nntree.—The defendant denied his liability for the slim of St Se 64 for attending on the child of a man named Fine- gan, *Web WAS run over by a cart. The Plaintiff had sent Ins bill of 1.2 s ed to his (defendant's father), and then to Miss Savage, of Woodside Form, for. the same child, and when he did not get paid seat him a bill for 2s 6d. He had never told plaintiff he would pay for his services to the child.—ln answer to his Honour, the defendant admitted that the child WAS run over by his father's cart, and that he °saw the plaintiff in his shop immediately after the acci- dent. On learning thartonly the child's arm Was ran over, he at once left because his father was anxious to know what bad happened.—The plaintiff said the defen- dant told him to do all he could for the child, and he would see him Pod.—Defendant : No such thing—Upon the de- fendant objecting to an item of 4s 6d, plaintiff said he would withdraw it. It belonged to defendant's mother-in- law, who had been in rather difficult circumstances. Ihe defendant had promised to pay it.—His Honour reduced the account by 14s 6d, and ordered payment of the remainder lobe made in 14 days.

BREACH OF TIE CANAL BOATS Acr.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. Joseph Chambers, of Odd Rode near Sandbacb, was charged with haring committed a breach of the Canal Boats Act, by allowing persons of the mate Red female sex of the ages of 14 and 12 respectively, to use the cabin of the boat owned by him as a sleeping place. Thomas Boot, inspector of Canal Boats to the Runcorn Commissioners proved the case and the defendant wee fined be and costs IL 6d.

ST. HELE.NSPAWI CHURCH: GIFT BY SIR GIL- BERT GREzNALL.-It having been decided to carry out extensive alterations to the St. Helens Parish Church, at an estimated cost of £1,500, Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., has contributed a sum of £5OO to the fund.

ANOTHER CANAL MYSTERY AT RIINCORN.—On Thursday afternoon, the body of a man, in a shock- ing state of decomposition, was found in the Bridge- water Canal at Runcorn. With the exception of having a pair of clogs, and a pair of socks, the body was. nude, and the features were unrecognisable. The body awaits an inquest at the mortuary. SHOCKING OUTRAGE IN A' RAILWAY CARRIAGE. --A sensational affair is being investigated at Stockport. A married wom:,n named Isabella Lloyd ' was found insensible in a rrittge of the Liverpool train arriving at midnigl. on Thursday at the Cheshire Lines Station, Stockport. • She was luau exhausted condition, with her head injured. After I being at the Infirmary for some tiMe she stated that between Liverpool and Warrington she was molested by two strange ,men, and remembered no more till she found herself at the Infirmary, where she now lies. THE Iloma IRON TRADE.—There has been .an im- provement in the English iron market during the past week. The Glasgow warrant market has been firmer, and prices have improved somewhat from the bottorn point of the previous week. Scotch i makers' iron s steady, but with only a quiet de- mand. Closing buyers of warrants on Wednesday were 44s 3id cash and 44s 6d a month; sellers, 44s 4d cash and 44s 7d a month. There has been a rather better feeling in the northern iron trade, and Pig metal has been stronger in price. No. 3 being 35s 9d for prompt delivery, and 36s 6d for spring and the early part of the summer by second-hand holders.—lron.

CROFT HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.--A tea party and dance in aid of the funds of the above society were held at the Board School on Saturday even, when there was a large attendance. Shortly after. six O'clock about 150 persons sat down to an excel- lent tea. The school-room was tastefully decorated, and choice plants were placed on the tables. The following ladies presided at the tea tables :—Mrs. Owen, Miss Ball, Mrs. Isaac Maines, Mrs. Joseph Whistan, Mrs. Farackerley, Mrs. James Houghton, Mrs. Green, and Mrs. Nathan Taylor, jun. Dancing commenced shortly before eight o'clock, and was heartily engaged in, Mr. Burgess, of Newton, supply- ing the music. Mr. F. W. Ball (the chairman of the society) officiated as M.C., and he performed his duties in a praiseworthy manner.

CLAIM OF FAIIkERS FOR COMPENSATION. A deputation of Cheshire members waited upon Lord. John Manners on Thursday to press the claim of the Messrs. Percival, farmers, of Preston Brook, to certain compensation from the local authority in respect of a loss of cattle. Last summer five cows, valued at £B5, belonging to the Messrs. Percival, were bitten by a dog affected with rabies. They were promptly destroyed on the order of a Government inspector specially sent down from London, but it was subsequently found that the county authority declined to make compensa- tion, saying that the statute did, not apply. The matter being put before the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster on Thursday, the deputation were in- formed that at the time the cattle were destroyed. the Privy Council had no powers, but inconsequence of a report which was made to them subsequently Parliament granted powers to the county authority to make compensation in such cases. Unfortunately the Act was not retrospective. SEQUEL TO .A. COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Thompson, an action was heard in which Dr. E. Casey, of Sutton, sought to recover £l4 138 from the Collins Green Colliery Company and Mr. Andrew Jackson, their manager, for sur- gical and medical attendance on four men who were injured during the sinking of the Bold Colliery shaft, onp the 19th May last. Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, St. Helens, appeared for plaintiff; Mr. Percy Davies, Warrington, represented defendants; and Mr. H. L. Riley watched the proceedings on behalf of Mr. Isaiah Pygott, the sub-contractor for sinking the shaft. On the date named a number of men were engaged in deepening the shaft, for which purpose blasting operations were resorted to. A man named Brown, was engaged "ramming" a shot when it exploded, injuring the four men who were in the shaft. As soon as possible they were raised to the surface, and Mr. Jackson said to a carpenter named Webster, "Go for a doctor." The man went for Dr. Casey, who at once proceeded to the colliery ; and ordered three of the men to be removed to the Cottage Hospital, and he went himself with the two carts conveying the injured men. Brown was so severely injured that it was found neces- sary to amputate his hand and extract the right eye, and. these operations were per- formed by Dr. Casey, assisted by Dr. KnowleA, St. Helens; a man named Fitzgerald had a compound fracture of the thigh, which had to be set; another named ,Prestage had both eyes burnt out; and another named Belly had some scalp wounds, but be was attended to at home. Dr. Casey was in attendance for about two months on the men at the hospital. Mr. Davies admitad the facts, but urged that Jackson did not say "Go for Dr. Casey," but "Go for a doctor."— Dr. Casey, the plaintiff, and John Webster, a carpen- ter at the colliery, gave evidence to the foregoing effect, after which Mr. Davies, for the defence, sab, mitted that the Collins Green Colliery Company- were not liable, as Mr. Jackson had no authority to • render them liable. The injured men were working- for Mr. Pygott, a sub-contractor, and not as colliers for the company. If his Honour ruled that Jackson was personally liable, he should submit that Pygott be joined as a co-defendant. After Mr. Jackson had given evidence that the men in the shaft were Mr. Pygott's men, His Honour expressed the opinion that he would much rather the parties settled it amongst them- selves, as if somebody had not sent for a doctor, feel- - ing!3 would have been outraged, and great com- plaints made of inhumanity. His flonour suggested an adjournment to see if the parties could settle saying he thought the effect would be very bad if he were driven to give judgment. The parties agreed to an adjournment with this object.

A FRANK CONFESSION.
EXTRAORDINARY LETTER FROAf A LOCAL PHYSICIAN.
To the Editor of the Liverpool Courier.
seldorn appear publicly in print ; hut the facts connected with my experience, which follow, are so striking that I venture to reproduce them entire.

Having had a long and general experience, both in hos- pital and private practice, of the worst affections, especially those tending to a general breaking down of the organic structure of the kidneys, indicative of that terrible scourge to human life, known to all as Bright's disease, I, perhaps, more quickly and certainly than the general practicionee would notice a decided change under an entirely new me- thod of treatment, and having departed from the reutine practice in jest such a case, and with astonishing results, I deem it essentially proper, both to myself and the public, that I should report it. Some time since I was treating Mrs Molyneaux. of 127, Crown-street, who had consulted a number of physicians, all of whom had diagnosed her trouble differently, assigning her ailments and general breakdown to different causes. When she came to me she was suffering acutely from in- tense pain in the lower portion of the beck, with great dis- comfort from the dropeical swellings in her limbs. She had bad headaches, sometimes on the top, but more often at the back of and through the eves, with flashes of light be- fore the latter, %veneering pains in the chest and palpita- tion of the heart. She had a sallow complexion, and the bowels were very irregular in their action, alternately loose and constipeted. With this she complained of a great in- disposition to exertion, felt more tired on rising in the morn- ing than when she went to bed at night, and had taken, as she expressed it to me, " barrels of medicine,' which only seemed to aggravate her condition instead of improv- ing it. I made a very careful examination of her case, and as- cribed all these ailments, and, as the sequel proved properly, to the kidneys being in a disordered condition, and this, in spite of the fact that she did not complain of their ac- tion. I found that the proper amount of urea and uric acid was not excreted; but that it was, and no doubt had been for a long time, retained in the circulation, causing blocd poisoning and many symptoms of apparent disease cf those organs for which she had been treated. No medi- cal man previous to myself had looked to the kidneys as the seat of the trouble. I gave her, in the course of five weeks, all the usual medicines that are known to the practitioner for diseases of these organs, and was very much discouraged that none of them were apparently of the slightest benefit. Happening at this time to see a letter published by Dr. W. E. Robson, L.R.C.5.1., late R.A , in which he gave his wonderful ex- perience in the use of Warner's Safe Cure, I determined, , as a last resort, to give this remedy a thorough trial, andl did so unknown to the patient. The medicine was given 1 as directed on the bottle, strict attention being paid to the 1 diet, and within one week there was a decided improvement, both in appearance and feelings of the patiene After con- tinuing it for some time a great chacge for the bette, was noticed, and a chemical and microscopical examination showed that large quantities of urea and uric acid were being thrown off by the kidneys. The patient soon lost her dropsical swellirge, the nervous tone was restored, the stomach was able to digest the food, and she. wlth her hinds and those to whom she was most dear, were more than surprised and gratified at the result of the treatment, and certainly she was rapidly regaining her former colour and spirits, and said she felt better than she had for years

previously. To me it has been an agreeable disappointment, because as I a medical man I was always unduly prejudiced against all so-called patent medicines; but after this experlmce with Warner's Safe Care, and after the testimony borne by Dr. Robson to its virtues. I feel it is my duty to give to you and, through you, the public, this statement, believing, as I do, that Warner's Safe Cure should be incorporated in the British Materia Medina, and that it to as near a specific for all diseases of the kidney as can be found. The public do not appreciate the fact, nor in many instances do physicians either, that a disturbance of the functions c f the kidneys is the first cause of the majority of the serious disorders or dis- eases affecting mankind, which never can be cured until the kidneys are restored to their healthy action. And I.Pcause the kidneys are neglected, I am satisfied is the reason the death- rate in this country is so high. Their condition is truly the hey to health, and not for one cl,:y should they be neglected. am, sir, yours respectfully. C. COLGROVE PERRY, M.D.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SITERDAY—Befere Alderman Burgess. WIFE NEOLECT.-30/111 Dutton, a tanner who had been living in lodgings in Rattermarket•street, was sent to prison for fourteen days for neglecting to maintain his wife, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Union. He had not contriblted towards her support for nine months. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alder.

man Harrison, and Councillor Greening. BEGGING: A SAD CASE.—RAohael Meredith wia charged with begging in Palmyra-square on Saturday eternoon. It was stated that she had once been in a good position at Welshpool, and she received a good character from the police, Chief Constable Hunt remarking that she was a sober, and, if she could get work, industrious women. Her husband, who was now dead, was formerly town clerk of Welshpool. The magistrates allowed her EI out of the poor box, with which to reach some frionde.—Tames Wil- liams, charged with begging in Bridge-street on Saturday afternoon, Was fined 5e and coats, and James Smith, for be- ing guilty of the same offence In Buttermarket-street, was sent to prison for fourteen days.—William Smith was smt to prison for fourteen days for begging in the Nlarket- place on Saturday night.—Bridget Murray, for a similar offence in Buttermarket-street, on Sunday, was sent to pri- nen for seven days—Richard Morris, an old man, also charged with begging, was ordered to be detained until evening. DanitICENNEsB —The following were dealt with for this offence :—Mary Towey, fined 5s and costs • James Thorp, fined 2s 63 and cos,s; Sarah Foden, fin id Sc and costs ; Jahn Noon, fined 5s and coals; Mary Ftannigan, fined 1.03 and cests. div.head: SHOCKING MISADVENTURE AT
div.p: SHOCKING MISADVENTURE AT
LOWTON.

A SISTER SHOT DEAD BY HER BROTHER. A painful occurrence at Lowton Junction, on Friday morning, occasioned great excitement throughout the district, and the peculiarly sad cir- cumstances by which it was surrounded was the ! cause of general expressions of sympathy for the family in which the event took place. As will be gathered from the evidence which follows, William l Jenkinson, a young man, 19 years of age, employed as a porter at Lowton Junction Station, was an his ! father's house at Parkside, when he picked up a ! single barrelled gun which had been in a corner of ! the house for several months, and, under the im- pression that it was not loaded, tried to fire an old ! ' cap " which he had taken from his pocket. The i gun, however, proved to be heavily loaded, and the 1 results were most disastrous. The charge, after 1 passing through the closed window of the kitchen, ! entered the head of Elizabeth Jenkinson, an elder sister of William Jenkinson, who was in the yard of the house. A fearful wound was caused, and the poor woman, who never recovered consciousness, ! died about an hour later. The mother witnessed the painful scene, and the son who fired the shot ' fainted a short time afterwards. Medical aid was ! summoned with all possible speed, but human 1 skill could avail nothing. The police were informed I of the occurrence, and the young man was taken ' into custody on a charge of causing the death of his sister. 1 Prisoner was brought before Mr. Merson, a county magi- ; strata, at an Occasional Court held at Warrington on Satur• ',day morning, and formally charged with causing the death I of his sister, Elizabeth Jenkinson, at Parkside, on the day ' before, by shooting her with a gun loaded with bullets. I Evidence was given by Mrs. Jenkinson, the mother, and the police, after which prisoner was remanded antil after the holding of a coroner's inquiry. . INQUEST AND VERDICT. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before 1 Mr. S. Aciehouse. coroner, at the Bull's Head Iran, Lowton Junction, on Monday at nom. 'The jury comprised—Messrs. !Henry Hibbert (foreman), Thomas Naylor, George Burrows, I Robert Rigby, Alfred Cotterill, Alexander Chisholme, Isaac I I llnsworth, George McCormick, Richard Walmsley, Thomas Egan, David Morris, Richard Latham, Michael McCoy, John Turner, and William Rirnmer. I The Coroner, addressing the jury, said : You are here to I inquire into the death of Elizabeth Jenkinson, who on Fri- day last, while outside the house where she lived, was killed . by a shot tired from a gun by her brother; William Jenkin- IWu. After hearing the evidence, and what I have to say en 1 the evidence, it will be for you to say how she came by her I death. The following evidence was then given : Julia Jenkinson said : lam the wife of Jolfia Jenkinsoe, who is a signal foreman in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway. I live at Parkside, Newton. Elizabeth was my daughter. She Was 21 years of age. I recollect Friday last, when in the morning I was in the kitchen with my son, William, and daughter, Elizabeth. I , This was about nine o'clock. I did not see tie gun before I my son had it. The gun does not belong to my husband, , but he borrowed it about eight months ago. It has not been used during that period. The gun has been kept near a i chest of drawers in the kitchen. My husband does not keep t any powder or shot. There was no powder flask in the house, and there were no caps in the house. I did net see who picked the gun up ; but I sew it in his hand. I don't I know if she went outside before the gun went off. The 1 firing of the gun was the first thing that attracted my atten- tion. At that time I turned round and I heard my daughter i cry "oh dear," and I ran to her. She was then outside and I I found her close to the window. She was on her knees. I There is a curtain in front of the window in the kitchen. I I don't know where my son went to. Mr. Kidd, chemist, came, but my daughter died about an hour afterwards. I never had any suspicion that the gun was loaded. The cap on the nipple of the gun was put on by my son. After the occurrence my son never said anything to me about it ; he only said "Is my sister dead ?" He did not stay long in the house, as he was running for the doctor.—P.S. Coin- mine asked if it was not a fact that the deceased's brother was" larking " with the gun and pointed it at his sister in the kitchen.—Witness said she did not see it.—P.S. Corn- mires asked if witness did not tell her son to put the gun I I down.—Witness replied that she did say something to that 1 effect before he fired.—P.S. Commins asked if the brother I was not pointing the gun at the sister when she said that.— Witness said she could not be sure, as she did not take par- ticular notice. She only saw him with the gun in his hand, and she told him to put it down —P.S. Commins said a re- port was out to the effect he had mentioned, and he only \ wanted to know lilt was correct.—The Foreman said he would like to know where the gun was got from.—Witness ' said her hushand borrowed it from a man named Ball. • John Jenlainson, signal foreman, said the gun came into his possession about 12 months ago when he borrowed it from a man named Ball. It was dred three or four times . shortly after he got it. Be knew the gun was loaded, but he had not had any powder or shot or caps of any descrip- tion in his house for eight or nine months. He gave about that time the powder dm., ti a man named Green. He I could not say why he bad kept the gun loaded in his house ' during all that time. He had not kept a cap on the nipple of the gun, and it had never been fired since. The gun was kept in a corner of the kitchen, partly hidden by a chest of drawers.—The foreman said he thought it was rather care- less for a loaded gun to have been kept inside the house for so long aperiod. Anne Warburton said :--I live next door to Jeukanson's. On Friday morning I heard the report of a firearm, and I came to the door. I sow Elizabeth Jenkinson lying on the floor under the window, bleeding from a wound on the head. I helped Mrs. Jenkinson to take her into the house. The deceased only said "Oh my." Before then I saw William 1 Jenkinson, who shouted to me "Oh Mrs.Warburton, do come and help me with my sister." I saw him go for a doctor and I saw him when he came back. He fainted when he came back. Mr. John Wesley Kidd, a chemist at Goll:flame, said:—On Friday morning last William Jenkinson came to my house. He got hold of my hand and said" Oh Mr. Kidd, will you come down to our house, I have shot my sister." I went with him and on the way from our house I asked him how it had happened. He said: I found a cap in my pocket and I was trying it on the nipper of the gun and it went off. I did not know it was loaded." ''l asked him if she was much hurt and he said ' he was afraid she was. He also said she was lying on the floor and bleeding. When I got to the house she was living, but she was unconscious, and she died ' in my presence about forty minutes afterwards. She was beyond all human aid. Vas shot had entered the temple and had gone ahrut an inch and then into the brain. A doctor was sent for, but all the doctors in England could not have done her any good.—By the Foreman : The son said he did not know the gun Was loaded. He also said ' that he tried the cap and it did not go off. He then lifted ' the hammer, pressed down the cap with hi., finger, and on palling the trigger again, the gun went cif —A Juror ob- served that the appearance of tee cep show( d that it was teo small for the gun. The cap would moire strongly pressing down. I P.C. Edward Spencer, stationed at :Newton, said : I re- ceived information of this matter at ten o'clock en Friday evening. I went to the house and saw the deceased lying

div.head: FXAMINER. S k TURDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1887.
div.p: THE FXAMINER. S k TURDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1887.

on a table in the house. She had a wound on the left tem- ple, just below the eyebrow. She skull was fractured, and she was quite dead. There were several marks of pellets on I her face, and the glass nf the window was broken. I ap- prehended her brother, Wm. Jenkinson, at half-past eleven I said: You are charged with causing the death of your sister, Elizabeth Jenkinson, by shooting her with a gun at nine a.m. this day. He replied : "I did not know the gun was loaded, and I did not know my sister was outside the house when I fired." He also stated "My sister took the gun from behind the drawers and placed it near the wall. I took it up and pointed it at her, but it had no cap on it at that time. My sister went out of the house. I had an old cap in my pocket, which I had had for twelve months. I put the cap on the nipple and pulled the trigger, but it did not snap the cap. I tried again, but it did not snap it the second time. I then pressed my thumb on the cap and put it firmly down on the nipple, and pulled the trigger again, and it went off." . .

The Coroner then proceeded to revievr the evidence, and in the course of a lengthy summing up, said the question for the jury to consider was, were the surroundings such as to justify them in saving that the girl came to her death by misadventure, or did they think that tbe brother Wil- liam Jenkinson was criminally responsible for the death of his sister. .

After a few minutes consultation in private, the jury re- tamed a verdict to the effect that the deceased came by her death by misaelventure, exonerating the brother from all blame. At the same time they wished the Coroner to speak to the father upon having had a loaded gnu so long in his house. The Coroner said be entirely agreed with the verdict of the jury. and he did not think that the son was in any sense to blame for the death of his sister. Addressing the _

father, the Coroner said: Mr. Jenkinson, so far as you are concerned the jury wish me to convey to you their ideae, and I gather from what they say that they think it was the most foolish thing for you to leave this gan leaded in the position you did, and for the length of time you did, in a place where all the children, and anybody could get to it. It was the most foolish and careless thing in the world. Here your lad, although exonerated from blame, has to live the remainder of his life, feeling in his own mind that he has killed his sister. It is a very serious thing indeed, and I quite agree with the jury that all persons having the care of firearms ought to take all the precautions in the world to see that they were not handled by anybody else, so dangerous are they unless skill was employed. The proceedings then concluded. THE PRISONER DISCHARGED.
mister.
Prisoner was again brought no at Warrington on Wednes:

day, before Mr. Marson, and formally charged on remand with causing the death of his sister.-. The Magistrate asked if there had been any enmity at all between any members of the family and the deceased.—PC. Spencer: No, they agreed very well together.—The Magistrate, addressing prisoner's Father, asked what occasion he had to use a gun. —The father: I have no occasion, except for shooting a few small birds for stuffing purposes.—The Magistrate: When was the gun put away.—The Father: I should say it has been put away for about eight months—The Magistrate : Do you suppose it safe for you to leave a loaded gun in the house when you are away P—The Father: I do not. It was not safe, and I am heartily sorry this has occurred.— The Magistrate: It is all very well to talk about sorrow now. You were the first cause of the accident, and if you have any conscience it must trouble you to the end of your days.—The Fathsr: It does trouble me.—The Magistrate remarked that no one with any sense would leave a gun loaded. Any spertsman, or person in the habit of using a gun, would always fire off his arms before putting them away. It seemed that the Coroner's jury had brouv,ht in a verdict of misadventure, and he did not suppose, if he were te commit him for trial that anything more would be done with him. They could scarcely take up a newspaper with- out reading of such foolish pranks as people pointing guns at each other without knowing whether they were loadrd or not. Prisoner would be discharged. but it was to be hoped that what bad happened would be a caution to him.

After further play, Tboroley. Lloyd, and Jones headed a rush of the Warrington forwards, Grey having to save. Bate, :gather, Molyneaux, and Ashurst worked the ball close to the Aspull line, where a scrimmage was formed, and on the ball becoming loose Thornley picked up and dashed over the line. but the try was disallowed. Grey relieved the. pressure by kicking into touch near the quarte-flig. Ashurst received the ball from the line out, and made slight headway, play again raging near the visitors' lins. Boardman made a futile drop at goal, and Freeman and Grey cleared their lines. The home forwards, headed by Jones, Ashurst, Adamson, and Lloyd, kept up the pressure, Seddon affording relief by punting into touch. Eeddon now put in a nice ran and kick, and Grey following up ran the ball to the home quarters, Unsworth bringing him down nicely. Grey got hold from tae scrimmage and Licked to Jolley, that player returning into touch. Hackett now passed to Mather, who gained a lot of ground, but Grey responded by a good kick, and fol- lowing up collared Unsworth with the ball in his possession. Adamson. Thoruley, and B.?lshaw now headed a splendid dribble, but lost possession of the ball, and Grey kicked to Jolley, who again returned into touch. Play now for some minutes was of a very even character, Warrington having rather the best of the cc-immagipg. Bate ' gained possession and ran round the scrimmage, and pissed to Boardman, who was collared by Taylor. before he could get away. Adams m was next conspicuous in the , line out, and Janes made a good dribble' when half-time was called, the ball resting in centre, and the score standing —Aspull three minor points to Warrington nothing. Early ' • in the mecum! half M ither obtained a Wee kick near the vis- itors' quarter flag. and Boardman taking the place kick made a good bid for goal, the ball going just wide of the posts, a dead ball being registered. Hindley dropped out, Mather returning and following up charged down Taylor's kick Hackett now passed to Mather, who repassed to Unsworth, the latter player apparently having a good chance to More but was collared by Prescot close to the line. Free- man afforded temporary relief by a short kick Into touch, but the home front rank, led by Adamson, Ashurst, and Molyneaux, again took play on to the visi- tors' line : and after a series of tight scrimmages, Aspull were forced to touch down. Aspull were now allowed three free kicks in rapid succession, but gained very little ground, the kicks being returned by Bate and Adamson. Seddon intercepted a pass intended for Unswortb, and made a good run, being brought down by alnther. The visitors now worked the ball to the home lines for the first time during the second half, but their stay was of short duration, the Warrington forwards clearing their lines in grand style, and Mather took the play to centre. Molyneaux next obtained _ _

a free kick, by which a lot of ground was gained. Freeman passed to Taylor, who put in a short run and kick, but Jol- ley replied by one of his long pun's, the ball going into touch. Time was shortly afterwards called, the score , standing Aspull three minor points to Warrington two minor points. Teams :—Warrington : Full back, Jolley ; three-quarter backs, Unsworth. Boardman (captain), and Mather ; half-hacks, Bate and Hackett; forwards, Moly- neaux, Adamson, Ashuret, Jones, Belshaw, Thornley, Lloyd, Holland, and Potts.
