Smith, Shorrock, Gregory, Hinciley, and Bond. WARRINGTON V. ASPULL.

Warrington sent a team to Aspull on Saturday that was weakened by the absence of Fair. Turner, Gilbert, Jolley Barna., Massey, Rigby, Hough, and W. Dillon, the first, named of these taking part in the county match at Man- chester, the other being mainly on the sick list. The substitutee, however, pla,yed well and the result was a well. contested and pleasant game in the presence of upwards of 3,000 spectators. H. Ashton lest the toss, the only disadvantage of this being that the Aspull team played with the sun in their favour. Frank Turner kicked off, Hulme being collared before he could return. From a good pass by the last named player, Bullogh put in a good run, but was smartly collared by Speakman. The Aspull forwards now played with great spirit, their efforts to score being frustrated by Ratcliffe saving well. Cartwright next made matters look dangerous, but Speakman relieVed grandly. Soon after a dead ball came about by a huge punt from Seddon. Apiece of good passing wan here witnessed on the pat of the visi- tors backs. Whittle in the first place passing so Haselham, who transferred to Ratcliffe, play raging in the home 25. A combined dribble was next on the board, the home for- wards taking the oval to centre. From a pass by Antrobus Haselham failed to pick up, but with a splendid dribble took the ball in clime proximity to the goal line. Scrim- mages were formed in this position, which ultimately ended in a touchdown in favour of the visitors. From the kick out Davies obtained a free kick, Lawson gaining possession and kicking to touch. Whittle next got hold, and gained a lot of ground by judiciously kicking up the field and tack- ling Bullogh before he could return. Ratcliffe further im- proved this by having a free kick allowed him, ending in Pilkington being compelled to bring into requisition the saving dance. Some give and take play ensued from the kick out. Howell got hold and made a nice run, but Davies proved a stumbling block to his progress. The visitors, by a strenuous effort, next made headway, a combined dribble taking place when the hall was loose, which resulted in an- other minor being scored to the credit of the capholders. Pilkington kicked out, the ball rolling into touch. A rush I by the home forwards took the ball to the visitors 25, Ap- pleton's aid being called in requisition, and be grandly steered the ball out of danger. On the ball becoming loose, Bullogh made a determined effort to score, but Speakrnan foiled this, which brought abcut half-time, the score being—Warrington, 3 minors; Aspull 1. On re-starting Pilkington kicked off. Haselham putting in a good return to touch. Cragan smartly collared the fullback before he could return. Law- son, Creston. and Bramwell now headed the home forwards from the halfway flag, the first-named crossing the line, the kick at goal failing. Turner kicked oat, and the home forwards forced play to the visitors' lines, Appleton kicking the ball dead. Frank Turner again kicked off, and a scrim- mage being formed, Antrobus broke away, and with the aid of Davies took the oval to the home 25, where a good chance of scoring was spoiled by Pilkington kicking to touch. The home forwards gradually worked the ball down the field, a dead ball resulting from a kick by Seddon. Re- starting, Seddon passed to Bullogh, who made a dashing I run, being collared by Speakman. Antrobus passed to Rat- cliffe, who was collared by Howell ig the visitors' quarters. LI Appleton shortly afterwards was compelled to teach down, andtimelwas called after 70 minutes of play, the result being, Aspull 1 try and 5 minors, Warrington 3 minors. The game was a well-contested and pleasant one, the forwards on both sides playing an extremely fine game, Davies, Ashton, and I Cragan, on the Warriegton side, and Lawson and Croston for Aspull, being the pick. Whittle and Antrobus quite surprised everyone with their masterly style of play, pass- ing with excellent judgment The rest of the backs also played well, Speakman in particular playing an exceed- ingly fine defensive game. liulme,Bullogh, and Pilkington played a fine game on behalf of the home team. Teams._4pUhl Pilkington, back; Tucker, Seddon, and Bullogh. three-quarter backs ; Hul me and Cartwright, half backs ; Haydock, Lawson, Baxendale, Hesketh, John Lind- say, James Lindsay, Croston, Monks, and Bramwell, for- wards. Warrington : Appleton, back ; Ratcliffe, Hasel- I ham, and Speakman, three-quarter backs ; Whittle and Antrobus„ half backs ; Graham. Littlewood, Davies, Povey. in front of the Earlestown posts. S Mania finally scoring by a swift low shot. Appleton male a good attempt to stop the leather—rendered difficult by the crowding of the backs upon him, but though he touched the ball it went threugh the posts. The supporters of the Golborne team cheered most enthusiastically, and threw up their hats and waved sticks without number. This was 20 minutes from the commencement. The Earlestonians restarted the game amid cries of " Play up Earlestown," and the excitement visibly increased. A visit was paid to the Golborne quarters, where W Shaw and Siddeley were robbed of the bail, when there were good opportunities of passing to other members of the team, and an attack on the Earlestown goal resulted in the leather being headed just past the posts. Following I some loose play by the 7aariestown half-hacks Appleton - had some difficulty in maintaining his charge, after which J Shaw rushed up the field, and a judicious pass enabled W Shaw to send in a stinging shot, which the Golborne goalkeeper only defeated by a strong kick. " Jimmy " Shaw directly afterwards shot into the keepers' hands, and he had only threw it away before Ellison had charged him through the uprights—a very near shave for Earlestown. I Play was sabsequently at the Earlestown end, the Golborne I backs and half-backs playing splendidly. The Earlestown forwards exhibited selfish play, and several times allowed their opponents to rob them of the ball, but after some pass- ing by Sint, W Shaw, Siddeley, and J Shaw, the latter almost scored by a swift low shot, the ball go- ing out by a few inches. Half-time was then called with the score—Golborne one goal, Earlestown none. For about about five minutes after the re-start Earlestown had by far the best of the play, and a strong attack on the Golborne goal resulted in Whalley passing the ball to Elli- son, who shot it in front of the goal, and J Shaw equalised the score amid load cheering. The pressure was kept up by the Earlestown forwards, and a strong shot by J Shaw was headed back from right under the Golborne goal. At this time Whalley received a severe injury to his ankle, which necessitated his retirement from active play, He went to keep goal while Appleton played half back, but the change worked disadvantageously. For some time the Earlestown team severely pressed their opponents, the Gol- borne goalkeeper and backs having to work hard to prevent increased scoring. After shots by J Shaw, Siddeley, and Elitism bad been repelled, J Shaw scored what almost every- one considered a legitimate point, and the cheering was prolonged when Earlestown bad taken the lead, as was then thought. The goal was, however, disallowed, presumably on account of "off side" play, but the decision was received with marks of disapproval from the spectators. The Golborne left wing couple—who played well throughout the game, ran the leather into the Earles- town quarters, and from a beautiful centre by R.Hembrough, Cottam rushed up and scored a second goal amid loud cheers. Earlestown again pressed their opponents, but the latter troubled the Earlestown backs, and when another score appeared likely Whalley saved in an almost miracu- lous manner. The ball was at once taken down the field, and from a goad pass by Ogden, J. Shaw again sent in a stinging shot, which scored, and once more made the teams level, amid every manifestation of enthusiasm. Earlestown still succeeded in pressing their opponents, and the brothers Shaw and Ogden, made good attempts to notch a leading point, until Sims sent in what appeared ta be a certain score, but one of the Golborne backs knocked the ball back with his hand, amid some hooting. From the free kick an exciting scrimmage followed, and J. Shaw again sent the leather through the goal, to the delight of the supporters of the Earlestown team, but the goal was again disallowed. Five minutes later, however, from a free kick by Sims, a scrimmage took place in front of the Golborne posts, and Sims and Ogden rushing up scored an unmistakeable goal. The subsequent play was in favour of Earlestown, but in the last three minutes the Gotborne forwards rushed up the field, and 8 Cottam made a long shot at the Earlestown goal. Whalley, owing to his injury, failed to reach the ball, and it rolled through the pests—a very easy goal, which made the teams level. The cheers of the Golborne supporters had scarcely subsided before time was called, with the result a draw—three goals each. The two teams will consequently have to meet again.

- RUNCORN GRASSHOPPERS (" A " TEAM) v. WEAVER VIEW ROvEßS.—nis match, under Association rules, was played at Frodshana on Saturday, the Grasshopers winning a plea- santly-contested game by one goal to nil. SUTTON FREE WANDERS V. FARNWORTH (2ND).—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday last. At the call of time the score stood: Sutton, one goal and two roicors, to Farnworth, one goal and one minor. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL V. WYCLIFFE FOOTBALL CLI3I3.—T his match was played on the ground of the former ' on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the school by three tries to nil. The tries were got by Preston, Fisher, and Scotson, who played well throughout. WARRINGTON CATHOLIC UNITED V.WARRINGTONWANDER- ERS.—The above teams played a return match on Saturday, which resulted in an easy victory for the United bv one goal, one try, six minors and two disputed tries to the 'Wan- derers three minors. Lally and McHugh played a good game for the United, and the forwards proved as usual to be in good ferm. RUNCORN RECREATION v. Sorrow. The Recreation journeyed to Sutton on Saturday to play off their return fixture with the above club, but with a poor team, J Clare ! and W Woodward, backs, and Hampson, Worrell, Massey,l and Rathbone, forwards, being absent, while the home team , were well represented. After a good game the match ended in a draw. Score—Sutton, 2 minors; Recreation, nil. WIDNES V. BlRCH—Played at Widnes on Saturday, the ' home team winning by tyro goals. one try, and eight minors, to one try. Time game throughout was well contested, in the first half especially; hat in the second, play was rather tame, only two minors being scored. The tries for Widnes were obtained by Plumpton (2) and Harding, and the goals were neatly kicked from easy positions by Farrell. Holds- worth secured the try for Birch, and Ferriman failed at the place. All played well on both sides. It would be invidi- ous to select from the Widnes backs. In the forwards, how- ever, Kiddie, Smith, Bingham, Hughes, and Fogg were fre- quently conspicuous ; whilst Allen, Bainbridge, and Holds- worth were the pick of the visitors. Teams :—Widnes : Bingham, back ; Harding, Plumpton, and Penuington, three-quarter backs ; Farrell and Harwood, half backs ; Kiddie (captain), Smith, Woods, Ridyard, Hardman, J Bingham, Hughes Fogg, and Perdin, forwards. Birch: Hesford, back ; Allen, Lithgow, and Wheeler three-quarter backs ; Higginbottom (captain) and Holdswortb, half I backs ; W Higginbottorn, Bainbridge, Ferriman, Beck, Harrop, Abbey, Cheetwood, Boucher, and Jackson. for- wards. RUNCORN V. CASTLEFORD.—The premier Cheshire Rugby , team went up to Yorkshire on S iturday, to meet the Castle- I I ford fifteen, who hold a good reputation in the county of many ecru,. There would be fully 4,000 people on the I ground when the teams appeared. Runcorn being represented , by T Woods, back; W Riley, H C Speakman, and H Caw- ley, three-quarter backs; H Hughes and H G Andrews,' half backs; W H Broady. W Wright, W Hughes, W Faulk- ner, J Clarke, George Wainwright, J Barns, J Gatley, and 1 J Ford, forwards. Castleford : R Harrison, back ; C Horner, A Hartley, and W Hammond, three-quarter backs; Thompson and J Morton, half backs; W Phillips, J Dickenson, J Dale, W Castle, W Jenes, S Asquith, G Brooke, A Cockcroft, and C Hamilton, forwards. Referee, H Wigglesvrorth, Thornes F.C. Davies and J Lewis were absentees on the Runcorn side. Peter Dickenson was away from the home team, playing for his county. Woods at full back was in his old form, picking up from the feet of his opponents and saving grandly. Speakman did his work I very well, and frequently got dangerous, but he had a strong opponent to face; his drop-goal was a cool bit of play. Harry Cawley saved frequently, and did a lot of useful work. W Riley was quick on the ball, and took every chance that came in his way. The Runcorn half backs were streets ahead of Castleford halves in saving, running, , and passing, getting often to the home full back before they were stopped, anct had very hard luck in not scoring on several occasions. The forwards played together as one man. Their short passing completely lost the home team In the last twenty minutes of the game. In the loose Runcorn played the best game, but in the packs Castleford held their owe. A word for Castleford—they had only three backs that really did any work, Hanson, Hartley, and Horner. The two half backs mulled tbe.ball .every. time

they cot it, the Runcorn backs being on their track in an instant. There is no time to consider what a half back must do with the ball when he gets it. The play of the two halves showed this. Forward, Castleford are good, being a big strong lot of men, but lack any science. They cannot pass a bit, and it was in that department they were beaten On Saturday, and the capital score of two goals, one try, to 6 minors, was run up by Runcorn. again very prominent, and Haeledon by some dashing play obtained two tries in quick succession. Immediately after this Dearden dropped a goal, and Leatherbarrow obtained an excellent try. The game resulted as follows :—St. Helens, two g( als, four tries, and twenty minors; Liverpool Wan- derers, one minor. For the " Saints " the forwards played well to a man, Pennington, Borthwick, Ellison, Anders, and Leatherbarrow being most prominent; whilst all the backs displayed splendid form. For the visitors W Lonsdale. P H Morton, Goodman, Beszant, Hornby, and Dodd strove hard to avert disaster. Teams: St. Helens—A Tickle, back; E Foreman, J Halton, and W Hasiedon, three-quarter backs; T Finney and J Dearden, half backs; A BOrthwick, C Anders. J Harwood, L Kershaw, T Pennington, J Hamp- son, H. Ellison, and D M‘i.oughlin, forwards. Wanderers— J Moir, back; W Lonsdale, P H Morton, and S G HornhY, three-quarter backs; CF Dodd and W Morton, half backs; J Graham, Bezant, Goodman, Summers, E W Head, J Fraser, H Porter, and J W Baker. forwards. WARRINGTON V. ASPIZILL (" A " TEAMS).—The return fix- ture between these teams was played at Warrington on Saturday, in fine weather. over 2000 spectators being 'present. The home players were cmsiderably weakened owing to the first team taking away several of their best men. Aspull won the toss, and Ashurst kicked off for War- rington at 3-15. Thornley followed up well, and prevented a return being made, and a scrimmage was formed in the visitors' quarters. Grey got hold and put in a g:od kick,

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The meeting between Lancashire and Somerset at Whal- ley Range, on Saturday, was one of great interest, and par- ticularly to Warrington people, on account of their local team contributing Fair Turner to the forward strength of the Lancashire representatives. The home team was much weakened by the absence of Flowers, Valentine, Springman, and Banks, whose places were taken by Worthington, Withers, Little, and Andrews from the reserves The con- test was a close one, the Somerset men showing op much better than had been expected, and in the end coming off winners by a goal, two tries, and two minors to three tries and one minor for Lancashlre. The losers were weak in the matter of three-quarters, but in the forward division the two lots were pretty well matched. Among the best and most useful of the Lancashire forwar s was Turner, Eagles and Seddon being also worthy of commendation. On Saturday there were several notable matches played under Rugby rules. The international between Scotland and Ireland was brought off at Belfast, in the presence of over 6,000 spectators. After their brilliant defeat of Eng- land the Irishmen naturally had expectations with regard to this match, hat the Scotchmen proved too many for them. The play was stubborn and well-fought, but the home team were hard pressed all through, and in the end Scotland run out with two goals and two tries to nil. Yorkshire County also sustained a reverse on Saturday at the hands of Mid- dlesex. The contest took place at Bradford, and was wit- nessed by no fewer than 12,000 persons. It was in every respect a splendid game, being so closely contested, that it . . . . . . . . . .
was only in the last minute or two that the visitors scored the winning point. The final resnit was Middlesex three tries and two minors, to Yorkshire two tries and three minors.

PENKETH FCHOOL V. OLD AcKWORTH Boys.—Played at Penketh, on Saturday. The result was in favour of Pen- keth by two goals to one. WIGAN AND DISTRICT CHALLENGE CUP—SEMI- FINAL TIE. EARLESTOWN V. GOLBORNE.

The meeti-n-g-Of-t-he Earlestown and Golborne clubs in the semi-final tie of the competition for the Wigan and District Association Challenge Cur), en Saturday afternoon, occa- sioned a widespread interest amongst the supporters of the two teams. The match was played on a neutral ground, that of the Haydock Football Club, behind the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Hawlock, and as the weather was beautifully fine, over 2000, spectators welcomed the teams. The elevens were as follows :—Earlestown J Appleton, goal; G- Clough and ft Green (c.ptain), backs; J Whalley, J W Sim, and J Green, half backs; J Ellison and J Ogden, right wing; J Shaw and W Shaw, left wing; T Siddeley, centre_ Gol- borne :W Jenkinson, goal; T Kay and J Waddington, backs; R Davies, J Clarke (captain), and J Hernbrough, halfbacks; S Morris and S Cottam, right wing; J Flynn, centre; Hembrough and J Lowe, left wing. The umpires and referee were appointed by the committee of the Association, and were as fellows :—Urapires, Messrs G 11 Hunt (Haydock) and H Middlehurst (Ashton); referee,Mr F Norris, of Bolton. Siddeley kicked off about 3-15, and some exciting scrimmages ensued in mid-field, and Lowe was cleverly stopped by R. Green. Ellison, and Siddeley took the sphere to the Golborne quarters, but Flynn and R. Hembrough transferred play to the other end, where the defence was sorely tried. The brothers Shaw relieved with a good run, and passed to Ellison, who, when having a good chance, was tripped by Clarke. The referee allowed Earlestown a free kick, which was taken by Whalley, and the ball was kicked outside the Golborne posts, after a brief scrimmage. The Golborne team about this time had by far the best of the game, and severely pressed Earlestown. Some relief was occasioned by J. Sha•iv and Siddeley, and Kay delibe- rately kicked the ball out, when the Golborne posts were menaced, The Earlestonians kept up the pressure, and se- cured a corner kick, taken by Whalley, but the ball went on the wrong side of the posts by a few inches. The Gol- borne forwards dribbled the ball to the opposite end and secured a corner kick; Cottans landing the ball among the spectators. The Golborne team next exhibited some good combined play and seriously endangered their opponents' goal, but the defence was very good, Clough several times saving what appeared almost certain scores. J. Shaw was next conspicuous by a good run and a clever attempt to score, but the leather flew over the crossbar. A similar shot was made directly afterwards by his brother " Billy " —though the chance of scoring was a capital one. Lowe for Golborne again invaded the Earlestown quarters, and from a strong shot the ball struck the crossbar and reboun- ded into the field of play. A desperate scrimmage followed

THE OLDHAM MURDER.—After a trial lasting over four days, Elizabeth Berry, 31, a widow, was on Thursday found guilty at the. Liverpool Assizes of murdering her daughter, Edith Annie Berry, by administering poison to her on the let and 2nd januaty last, at Old- ham. The motives for the crime appear to have beon a desire to rid herself of the burden the child was to her, she having to pay about £lO a year for her daughter's maintenance out of her salary of .895. and also the wish to obtain the possession of a PUM of £lO for which the child was insured. div.head: WIDNES AND THE LIVERPOOL WATER SCHEME.
div.p: WIDNES AND THE LIVERPOOL WATER SCHEME.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Bard was held on Thursday morning, for the purpose of considering the Bill to amend the Liverpool Works Acts, &c. Mr F H Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs E Carey, S Sadler, H Gaskell, jun., J Taylor, F Heves, W T Husband, J Midwood, W W Gossage. Dr U'Keeffe, and J T Allen (clerk).—Mr Carey moved that the meeting having con- sidered the clauses and provisions in the Bill to amend the Liverpool Water Works Acts, and for other purposes, de resolve that the Local Board oppose the said Bill in Parlia- ment, and take all necessary steps, by petition or otherwise, as may be deemed expedient, and that all the costs, charges, and expenses incurred, and to be incurred, be paid out of the general district rate, or other funds applicable for the purpose. Mr Carey remarked that in opposing the Bill the Local Board had no desire to impede the Bill, or alter the agreement they had made with the Corporation, but in order that they might be entitled to watch that that agreement be not altered by accident or any of the parties interested.—Mr Gaskell vcended the motion. He thought it was necessary that the Board should be represented in Parliament, because many public bodies were opposing the Bill upon the very ground that Widnes and other places were to be supplied with water from the Vyrnwy Scheme. The motion was carried unanimously. The appointment of a depuOtion to attend the House of Commons was deferred until the ordinary monthly meeting. Subsequently a meeting of ratepayers was held, under the presidency of Mr Gessage, who moved that the decision of the Local Board be carried into effect. The motion was seconded, and carried unanimously.

div.head: SHOCKING REVELATION AT WIDNES._
div.p: SHOCKING REVELATION AT WIDNES._

Before Mr. T. 8. Timmis, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Annie S. Green, a young woman, was charged with threatening to assault and beat her husband, Joseph Green. Mr. Rideal, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff. Green, who is a stoker at the works of Messrs. Mathieson and Co., was married to his wife two years ago, and one child was the result of the union. Abont fifteen mouths ago they went to live with his wife's stepfather, but after staying a month Green left because he had to sleep on the floor,whilst his wife slept in bed with her stepbrother, 17 years of age. In April he again stayed 9 days with the stepfather, and slept on the floor each night without pulling his clothes off. One night he went upstairs and found his wife tubed with her stepbrother. When she saw him in the room she shouted for her stepfather, who came upon the scene and threatened to use violence towards him. On Saturday night last, after coming from the theatre, the de- fendant followed him and several friends into Wright's publichouse, struck him, and used most violent and abusive language towards him.—Several witnesses were called to corroborate; and the defendant said her husband was con- tinually annoying her, and had on several occasions thrown bricks over the wall of the yard of the house where she lived. He took her baby away on the 28th January, and on the Bth February he brought it back and placed it on the sofa. She had never troubled either him or his relations for anything, as she was able and willing to keep herself.—Mr. Tirnmis said the case was clearly proved, and sentenced the defendant to be bound over to keep the peace for 6 months, herself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each, or in default 14 days' hard labour. The woman went to gaol.
WIDNES COUNTY COURT. FRlDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Thompson.

DAMAGES FOR PERSONAL INJERY.Thomas Thornton, cooper, Victoria-street, claimed from Thomas Hawkins, greengrocer, Widnes-road, the sum of £2 19s, compensation for injury caused to his wife through the defendant's neg- lect.—Mr. George Rideal, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. C. H. Lewin defended.—lt ap- peared that on the evening of the 27th November Mrs. Thornton was walking along Victoria-street, when she fell over a pair of scales which had been placed on the foot- path. The scales belonged to defendant, and were in the shadow of his cart, which was standing in the road. In falling Mrs. Thornton severed one of the arteries in her left arm;and would never be again able to fellow her employ- ment as a washerwoman. The two boys in charge el the cart, after remarking that Mrs. Thornton would bleed to death if she were not at once taken to the Infirmary, drove away.—The defence was that the boys warned Mrs Thorn- ton of the scales, and that it was in consequence of her own carelessness and through being under the influence of liquor that the accident occurred.—Mrs. Thornton denied that she had had any drink during the day, and called several witnesses, who deposed to her sobriety.—His Honour gave a verdict for the plaintiff, with Costs. ACTIONS AGAINST THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.—Charles Rawsthorne, of Ditton, sued the London and North-Western Railway Company for the sum of £2 16s 4d, being the value of a cheffionier alleged to be damaged during transit from Manchester to Ditton en the defendants' line.--Mr. j. W. Knowles was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Preston, junr., represented the company. The plaintiff purchased the article of furniture, which was described as " mahogany veneer," from William Dreyer, 368, City-road, Hulme, Manchester, a travelling draper and furaiture dealer, of Manchester, some time during Decem- ber. The price agreed upon was £2 15s, and a further Is 4d was added for carriage and porterage. The company ad- mitted that the cheffionier WAS in sound condition, and the only question to decide was the amount of damage it had suffered when delivered to the plaintiff. As pro- duced in court the article was shattered very badly. Lever deposed that he purchased the chef- fionier from a wholesale house for £2 Is 6d, and he stated the article was now not worth more than 10s.—Jas. Weatherall, cabinet maker, Manchester, stated that it would cost £1 to £1 105 to repair the article, and that it would not then be rqual to new. In questioning this witness, Mr. Preston commented upon the gingerbread fashion in which the article was m ado, and Weatherall said it did not matter how it was put togsth2r so long as it stuck. (Laughter.) Evidence was called for the defence to show that not half of the damage 39 represented was done, and an estimate was put in from a practical cabinet maker named John Rathbone, of Albert-road, who stated that it could be repaired for 108. The company bad, however, doubled this estimate, and paid £1 into court in settlement of the claim.—Mark Prescot, a porter, and Mr. John Smith, stationmaster, Ditton, de- scribed the slight nature of the damage when they ex- amined the furniture, and Mr. Rathbone said it was the most " jerry " description of furniture he ever saw.—His Honour gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the full amount claimed, with costs, the railway company to take the cheffionier.
PRESENIATION TO THE REV. DEAN FINEGAN AT WIDNES.

THE SCHOOL BOARD CONTROVERSY. There was a crowded addience in the new schools con- nected with St. Bede's Chapel, Appleton on Inesday even- ing when a concert was given by the following local artistes :—Miss Leatherbarrow, Miss Lillie Leatherbarrow, Messre. F. Heves, J. Morrison, E. Wallington, and Dr. McCambridge. Miss Johnson was the acconwranist. The principal event of the evening, however, was the presenta- lion of an illuminated address to the Very Rev. Dean Fine- gan, the priest of the parish. The address was in the fol- lowing terms : " We, the undersigned, on behalf of the members and friends of St. Bede's, Appleton, beg to offer you our hearty congratulations on the dignity which has been conferred upon you by his Lordship the Bishop of Liverpool. We, who know your great abilities, can easily understand why you have been raised to the dignity of Dean of this exten- sive Diocese. Since you came amongst us you have earned our esteem and regard by the zealous manner in which you have laboured, both for our spiritual and tem- poral interests. The decoration of the church, the new bell, the completioe of the organ, and the new boys' school, are lasting monuments of the work you have done for this mission; and, in your public capacity, both on the School Board and the Board of Guar- dians, you have rendered signal service, not only in the in- terest of Catholics but in the interest of the ratepayers generally. With this address we ask your acceptance of a \watch and purse of money, as a slight token of our joy at the honour which has been conferred upon you, and we hope and pray that you may long be spared to continue the good work which you have so successfully inaugurated.—Signed on behalf of the subscribers, " ALCUIN Jwo. COWLEY. "Appleton, February, 1887. JOSEPH MORRISON." Mr. J. Morrison, who conducted the proceedings, made a brief speech in which he said he was pie:tied to be able to state that the funds had been provided not only by Catho- lics, but by many neighbours and friends who differed from them in religion had accorded them most generous support. (Applause.) The Dean had done sufficient work to enlist the sympathy and gratitude of every Catholic in the parish. and he was perfectly certain that if be were to leave next day he would leave behind him a lasting monument of his zeal and industry on behalf of Catholics since he came to Appleton. Alluding to Dean Finegan's labours as a mem- ber of the Board of Guardians, Mr. Morrison said that body I had recently shown its opinion of his services by making him chairman of the Finance Committee, feeling that as I long as they had him at the head of the spending depart- ment everything would be done with.dee regard to efficiency and economy, and above board. (Applause.) Although, Dean Finegan appeared to give universal satisfaction on the ; Board of Guardians, he could not say he was so successful ' on the School Board. The dean had been subject to a great deal of criticism, and of coarse nobody objected to fair criticism such as was used by the members of the board ; they could agree to differ and respect each others I motives, But the writers of certain letters publiehed in one , of the local papers, had evaded the question at issue, and had used coarse language to attack the Catholics of the district. Ele was sure that in these days of toleration any man who went out of his way to attack the religion of his neighbour stood self-convicted as a narrow-minded bigot. (Applause.) Mr. F. Reyes then made the presentation of the watch, the purse of gold (nearly £2O), and the address, accompa- nied by a f..w appropriate observations. I The Very Rev. Dean Finegan, who was enthusiastically received, said he accepted the testimonial with a certain amount of diffidence, well knowing that it was not deserved on his part, and that the words of the address, rather painted him in the position in which his people would wish to have him than in the reality. He could say honestly and with truth, that he had done very little; but if he had not done ae much as he wished, he had done his best. (Ap- Plasse.) After alluding to his parochial labours, the Dean ;mid a Catholic pries, never could stand still when the cause of education demanded his services, and if tale be true in general it was sill more tree at present. We were in an age when the demands of education pressed heavily noon the priests who had charge of parishes, and if he had not marched with the times in providing school accommodation

for the children of his parish be should have deserved their censure. As to his position on the Board of Guar- dians, so long as be had health and the means to go to Free- cot, and so long as the people of that district placed con- fidence in his services, so long would he endeavour to represent them. (Applause.) He had always acted on the principle of doing as much as he could for the poor of Widnes, consistent with justice and honesty to the rate- payers of the town. (Applause.) With regard to the School Board, he had been a member of that body for a longer period than he had been a guardian, and he was almost beginning to think that it was time for him to retire from the School Board. (Laughter.) Probably many per- sons thought the same as he did. (Laughter.) They could laugh as they liked over that, but be could assure them that he would be very glad to retire from the School Board at the earliest opportunity if a substitute could be got to supply his plac.. He had certainly enough to do. As to the criticisms that had appeared upon him, he claimed to be the personal friend of everyone on the School Board, but as long as he was a member he should fearlessly express his opinions and vote according to his convictions. (Ap- plause.) Courtesy and respect he owed ey'ryone, but he could not swallow his opinions to please anybody. He would endeavour in the future, as he had done in the past,to carry on educational work either there or elsewhere in the dis- trict, because be was fully convinced that we must be an educated people. (Hear, hear.) The time must come when it was the right of every child to be educated, and they must bring this education home to the poorest child as well as to the rich. (Hear, hear.) The members of the Board might differ as to the best means of carrying out this programme, but that would not matter in the least cemented 23 they were in the union of hearts to engage in carrying out the same work. There was not in England a School Board that had acted with more justice and impartiality to all the sects of which the community was ccmposed. (Ap- plause.) Moreover, the members were all personal friends, and might this friendship long last, and it would last to long as they acted gentlemanly towards each other. (Ap- plause.) The Dean concluded by thanking the subscribers to the testimonial, and mentioned several schemes for im- proving the parish, and paying a compliment to Mr. H. Wide Deacon for the practical interest be had taken in thifm.

But for the settlement which closes to-night members of the Stock Exchange would have found it difficult to occupy their time daring the past week as the attitude of "hands down" has been vigorously maintained during the past few days. There have been few fluctuations in any market, but the tendency, on the whole, has been upward,more especially so in those securities which are regarded as less likely to be influenced by another panic, although the intimate rela- tionship of every kind of security to sudden, falls is such that it is difficult te select a stock that would not be liable to stiffer from a recurrence of panic, not due to any cause but that of eympatby with the general feeling of the markets. I have called attention recently to several securi- ties which have touched the loweet depths they are likely to see for some years and believing strongly that the war scare was ungenuine, I have advocated purchasing in those rates, knowing that a sharp and permanent rise was certain to take place on the first removal of the feeling of uncer- tainty, and the course of the markets have fully justified my anticipations. The securities I have advocated were home and the west Americans, more especially railways. The feelings of relief, inspired by the result of the German elections and the indications of improving trade, are likely to cause a rapid rise on the present prices of securities and Investors.

There has been a slight move in the company world this week, the first in the field being two gold mines, as usual, ' but as these are so purely speculative and were simply brought out on account of the limit of time allowed by the contract, it is not necessary to eularge upon them. Home mine investors will be interested in learning that the Bor- rowdale Plumbago Mines and Manufacturing Company has been revived to work this important industry under the auspices of an influential board. This mine was first dis- covered in the sixteenth century, and has been worked from time to time, producing the only pure pencil pinuabago in the arced. The dividends in former times have been enor- mous, one year yielding no less than £118,870. In the north of England especially the opening up of this mine will-afford great satisfaction where its value has long been appreciated. 11

THOUGHTS ON TWO LECTURES.

Sir,—This week I have had the pleasure and privilege of listening to two good lectures, Mr. Tuckwell's and Mr. Eh Bleckly's. They had one thing in common—the quiet way in which the teaching of the Old Testament was set aside, ignored, or subverted. The rev. lecturer, amongst other things startling to an orthodox mind, showed us the skull of the oldest inhabitant—that Is the most ancient example of early man—of a distinctly gorillean type—quite unlike the Appollo-like Adam we have been taught to believe in. And the same havoc was wrought the Biblical chronology as had wrecked Mosaic anthropology. It was evident the rev, lec- turer was no "six-day ' man. That doctrine received its cenge in the evidence that one of the most recent of the life periods of the earth, comparatively a thing of yesterday, must be calculated by more thousands than Moses ever dreamt of. Mr. Bleckly also spoke of the great antiquity of our little world with an utter disregard to the o>inion of Arch. raker and his contemporaries, who derived their statistics from the pages of the Bible. He also condemned the berning of witches. Now, if this be not flying in the face of Scripture, what is? Now, sir, is belief, like the" service," going to the dogs? Is the sacred text to be dealt with in this manner? Has the Great Stone Book proved a touchstone on which the Bible has in this respect been tried and found wanting? It is quite time this question were settled. At present we are illogically mixing the method of Moses with the method of Euclid. Are the parents and teachers of the young justified I in continuing to do this on the old lines of the Mosaic nar- rative merely to have their teaching shattered and con- demned when the pupil comes to reason? If these dogmas cannot be maintained, would it not be better to say so, te face the difficulty, well knowing that no advance of science, no subsequent human discoveries can in any way destroy or ' mutilate the principles of true religion.--I am, etc., JOHN, PEERS.
Penketh, February 16tb,1887. THE JUBILEE AND THE CURRENCY.

Sir,—As new coins are to issue from the mint this year. allow me to seggest that a grand opportunity is offered for the rectification of our clumsy system of coinage. At. a congress of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, held i many years ago, all the countries then represented, agreed I to, adopt and introduce the decimal system. Our Govern- ment also proposed to deposit samples of our present coins (as relics !) in the British Museum, that posterity might see the difficulties with which their forefathers had to fight. ' The pound sterling was to be divided into 1,000 parts, to be called" mils," instead of into 960 farthings, the old four- fold nomenclature being reduced to a twofold one of florins and mils. To effect this, all that is necessary is the issue of a Royal proclamation, decreeing that on and after a cer- tain date (June 20th), the farthing shall represent the 50th part of a shilling instead of 48th. The florin, as yet the only instalment towards the new system, would in course of time take the place of a shilling in being the unit coin for purposes of calculation. The table would be 100 mils (10 cents)-1 florin ;10 florins-1 pound ; and the coinage : Gold. 10 florins (£1), 5 florins (108.); Silver, 2 florins (43.), •1 florin 50 (35.), 1 florin (25.), 50 mils (Is.). 25 mils (6d.), 10 mils (1 cent, 20.); Bronze, 5 mils (1-10th of 1s), 2mils (id.) For a time, a threefold nomenclature might be used of pound, shilling, and mil, LS 12s 60. becoming £5 12s 27m.; but as the public got accustomed to calcula- ting by mils, the great advantage of combining the pound and shilling columns into one, of fibs ins, would become ap- parent to all, thus :-56 florins 27m. The same 81112, in mils 5,627, could be reduced in an instant to 5 poundei 6 florins, 2 cente and 7 mils,-56 florins, 27 mils. The only alteration in the value of our present coins would be in the bronze tokens and. the 3d bit, and the diff- erence would be so trifling, that only taxes, licences, stamps, &c. would be affected. A new tariff of these would be issued, whereby the loss or 1-6th on each penny would be compromised in the case of the two former, by count- ing sums under 31 as 4 mils to a penny, adding 1 mil to sums from al to 9d, 2 from 9d to 15d, 3 from 15e1 to 21d, and 4 from 21a1 to 24d: a tax of Os 3d would become 36. 13 ;a 9d bill of exchange 38 mils, and so on. Stamps would be revalued, thus rnils,.ld-5, 14-1-7, 21-9, 244 11. 31-13, 4d-15, sd-20, &125, 9,135m115. lhe trifling loss on some would be amply compensated for by the gain on I the others, especially on the penny stamps ; the little trou- ble caused by these slight alterations woold be far outbal- anced by the enormous amount of time and labour saved in business ; and the difficulty now felt, with regard to the circulation of foreign bronze coins, would be got over, for 4 mils would be the exact equivalent to the Jersey pepny, the French, Belgum, and Swiss 10 centimes. the Spanish 10 centimos, the Italian 10 crintesimi, the 0-reek 10 lepta, and the Roumanian 10 hauls. As a national memorial of the Jubilee, and as one that will not touch the pockets of the people, nothing could betier fulfil its object, so long as the poorest of Her Maj— esty's subjects possessed an humble mil. I am, Sir, yours truly, W. W. HARDWICKE;
MR. JOAN BRIGHT AND DISE-STAi

LISEIMENT IN WALES. The following letter has been received by a War- rington correspondent from Mr.. John Bright, whose attention Was drawn to a statement made in a ser- mon by a local Baptist minister.. The correspon- dent informed Mr. Bright that the minister, while speaking on the subject of conversion, said that it was possible for a man to hold certain opinions from youth to old age, and at last to change his opinions on the same subject, and then mentioned that "John Bright, the other day, actually went into the lobby and voted against religious equality in Wales.' Mr. Bright's reply is as follows ; - " Alexandra Hotel, London, February 24th, 1887. —Dear am sorry you should have a Baptist minister so ignorant or so unjust.. The vote was not against religious equality, but a vote to post- pone a particular motion, in order that one of more pressing importance might be considered. The Welsh Church question will keep, and another day for the discussion may be secured. The rules of the House of Commons require amendment, and the amendment, if effected, will enable even the Church question the more certainly to be discussed. —Youra very respectfully, Town Ilnsnirr."

div.head: DISASTROUS_ COLLIERY_ EXPLOSION
div.p: DISASTROUS_ COLLIERY_ EXPLOSION

IN WALES.--38 LIVES LOST. A terrible explosion occurred at the Cwlch Col- liery, Rhondda Valley, about seven o'clock on Fri- day night. The report shook buildings a mile away, and even on the Penrhyn mountain, miles off, houses shook. Pit carriages were shot up, and three persons on the lop of the pit shaft where in- jured by the flying debris. There were at the time about 52 men below, the residue of the day shift, who had not come up. Sbveral hundred men had' just before come up, and by pure accident of cir- cumstances 200 had not gone down in time, being delayed by the carriage coming up with coal. The whole of the interior of the shaft was wrecked, and for four hours it was found impossible to make any descent. There can be no doubt the explosion is due to gas, but how the accumulation occurred is a mystery, as the manager was down during the clay and all was safe. The pit bank was crowded with men's relations and friends, and the spectacle was piteous in the extreme, women and children mourn- ing the fate of relations. The colliery has been working seven years, and the owners are Watts and Company, proprietors of the nisei', and other col- lieries. The men at Guy's colliery, who were about going down to work, were induced to go to Cwtch to render assistance. A force of police from Pontypridd was speedily on the spot. The managers of other col- lieries hastened to offer assistance, and there was a mere than sufficient supply of medical aid. It was ascertained that 52 men were down, but owing to the exhalations of 'gas, and the damage to the descending gear, the effort to extricate them. could not be made for several hours. The rescue parties were at last lowered in a bucket, and shortly after. midnight 29 men had been brought out uninjured, and eight others more or less cut and burnt. The exploration was continued late into Saturday morning, and late and dark though the hours were, there was painful excitement, and each of the in- jured men who were first brought up were accom- panied home by mournful crowds. Some of the deal were also got at in these hours. They lay nearest the pit bottom on the north aide. It be-- came abundantly evident that the explosion had occurred on the north side of the 4ft., the men working in the opposite or northern direction being comparatively unbuped, but they had to wait three hours before they could get up, On Monday morning the explorers had gone into the interior of the north side of the workings, over 1,000 yards from the pit bottom, and close to tie place where the whole of the =recovered dead worked. The two air bridges blown down we're replaced temporarily, and trellices set up to restore ventilation. Then by twos and threes the dead, burnt and disfigured, were brought out a their working places. Sir W. T. Lewis, chairman of the South Wales and Monmouthshire Benevolent Fund, and Mr. Owen, the agent, were present. All the miners in this colliery belong to the fundt, and the claim will amount to £1,500. The opinion gains ground that the explosion was due to blasting, as this operation is usually carried out between the ascent of the day men, and the descent of the night shift. The desCeut was delayed, owing to the usual signal not being received. • The inquest on the 24 bodies, recovered from the Ynishir Colliery was opened on Monday. There had been no further bodies recovered up to noon. The inquest was adjourned for a month after evidence of identification had been given. It has been ascertained that the death roll will not exceed 38„

The "Standard" publishes the following, dated Rome, Thursday night:—The destruction is widespreadtbe towns and villages in and neat the sea coast having suffered most severely, and It is now estimated that, in addition to a vast amount of property, fully 2,000 lives must have been sacri- ficed. Of these, 300, were crushed by the fall of the tower of the church at Bajardo. The smaller towns and vil- lages suffered more than the large cities. At Alassia two persons were killed, and 15 badly hurt. Communication with Corsica has been intercepted, and 14 localities are cut off from communication by the injuries done to the wires. He reminded the House that the proposal of the hon. member for Cook was to exempt votes in supply from the action of the rule closing the debate, and he supported it because he felt indisposed to band over the public purse to any Government.—The CHANCELLOR of the Damp:63En denied that the object of the Government was to stifle discussion. div.p: F.RODSHAM.

• HOME MISSIONS. - The annual meeting of the Home Missionary Society in connection with the Wesleyan Methodists was held in Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Mon- day evening, when Mr. John Nicholas, of Frodsham Bridge, presided. The Rev..V. E. Page, of Chester, attended as the deputation, and in a very interesting manlier dwelt upon the several objects which the society bad in view in the propa- gation of the Gospel of Christ to the heathen at home and abroad. The Rev. E. Mosscrop read a report of the receipts during the past year, from which it appeared that the total amount was £l2 Bs 9d. The amount of receipts for the r present year was already £9 03 41

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT COCKFIEDGE MILL. . .
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT COCKFIEDGE MILL. . .

A shocking accident OC-ca-u;ed at Cockhedge fac- tory at about noon on Thursday, a young man named James Turner, 33 years of age, who was employed by Messrs. Armitage and Rigby as a strip- per and grinder, receiving injuries from which he died at the Infirmary the same afternoon. It ap- pears that deceased, in company with two men named Thomas Naydon and Edward Hill, went on the roof of one of the cardrooms to take down a dust pipe. Deceased was asked by Naydon to hold a ladder for him. In doing so deceased caught his heel against a skylight, and, when trying to re.. cover his balance, caught his other foot against it. The consequence was that he came down on the skylight, which broke, and he fell through to the door of the room below, a distance of about ten feet, on to a bobbin box. Me exclaimed" Oh!" and never spoke again. The poor fellow was at once removed to the Infirmary, where he was atten- ded to by Dr. Richmond. At half-past three the same afternoon he died from his injuries, which were chiefly of the head and neck. Deceased was a single man. An inquest will of course be held.

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE IRISH
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND THE IRISH
LAND QUESTION. TO TIM EDITOR OF "THE EXAMINER."

Sir,—Last Friday night Mr. Ho"Wes,TiTici;.lecture on Ireland and Home Rule, quoted a part of Lord Salisbury's speech in the House of Lords, something to the effect that, if the tenant farmers of Ireland were unable to pay their rents in accordance with the stipulation of the Land Act of 1881, the State should be held responsible, and make up the de- ficiency. Mr. Howes then added that not one of the Liberal Unionist leaders had from that date (August 1885) said one word in condemnation of that speech. Knowing this to be nntrue, I gave him a friendly interruption, and contested the point. In answer to Mr. Howes, I said' Mr. Cham- berlain had spoken in condemnation of that princi- ple, from which he still dissented. Well, consider- ing that Mr. Howes was fully occupied' if giving lectures, that he was dealing very unfairly towards Mr. Chamberlain, whose Radicalism none can doubt, and who is known to be entirely opposed to any system of dealing with the question of land ,that would have put the risk on the British taxpayer, I considered it my duty to write to Mr. Chamberlain informing him of the rash statements which Mr. Howes was making. I had intended tcs have sent him a report of his lecture, but was unable-to, do so, as you were compelled to leave it over till next Saturday. I have received, in reply, the enclosed letterfrcm Mr. Chamberlain.-1 remain, yours respectfully, L. Surma-Tn.

(BNCLOGURE.) 40, Prince's Gardens, S.W. February 21, 1887. V Dear Sirl do nott think it is in the least neces- sary for me'to• defend' myself against the statmuents- ,of an itinerant lecturer. In any case I could not do, Iso without seeing the-exact words used by Min., My views in reference to, the land question in Ireland have been fully stated in my two last speeches de- livered at Hayrick and:Birmingham, and if you will refer to these you will see that I am entirely op- posed to putting risk on the shoulders of the Brit- ish tax-payers, and thatp I have a plan for-dealing with the subject which will! avoid this nacessity, and at the same-time. will seeure the great•object of making the tenanta•owners ot their land. I remain of the opinion,. In spite of Mr. Howes' assurances, that Mr. Gladstone's land bill would havo involvedthe country in the greatest possible risk of 'loss; and all that hats occurred since con- firms-the opinions which -I have publicly expressed on the subject. I may add that ,I am having all /;my speeches on the Irish question collected and re -published, and whenthe volume is out- P wilt send you a copy.— Yours truly, Mn.L. Sutcliffe,

I‘ITHODIST CON VENT lON AT WARRINGTON.

On Monday -evening a Methodist : local home mis- sion convention was hen in. Bold-I ;treat Wesleyan Schoolroom, Warrington, inr the ra irpose of bring- ing 'before the Methodiste,of thet ten vn the claims of the missions nowt:being worked suct tessfully in the town. The chair was taken by the Rev. G. E. Cut- ting, and there was a large attend lance, including representativee •of 'Bold-st, B'ewsey• rd, and' Sankey Bridges Chapel 4 and ofmarions MILS .sion societies.— The Cmarnmas said it was a great sat Infection to him to take part in a meeting of Christian wort :era, who were so sucressfally engaged in evangelistic wor k in various parts of the town. All rernembered.with much I delight the won- derful things of the October COnvention , and he trusted that the present gathering would share, beneath the earn e divine guidance, a similar blessing. He 'believed a new era had been entered upon in, coanectiom with Warrington Methodism, and the missions at fdall-stret it, at Silver-street, at Mill-lane, at Batterslayelane, and the yery,succsseful ragged school movement in Bewaey.streett, were good tokens of the recent aggressive spirit of the followers of John Wes- ley. (Applause.) It was a great encouragement to the friends at Bewsev-road and, Silver-street that about 300 ragged children, as precioust•in the sight of the Saviour as other childreni had been gathered into the Dailam-lane chapel, and were being taught the elements o'l religion by Mr. Skelland And his band of helpers. (Her hear.) He deprecated running on sleepily,. in the deep,. hard nits of monotony and routine, alai believed a more successful time f had started already. To communicate life, workers must possess life. He appealed to all who were disposed to stand aside and oriticize to enter. themselves into ea:mesa practical work in benefiting the bodies and souls of perishing men, and they would be a means of eaccoragement,, instead of obstruction, to other workers. He wao, proud to introduce to them representative] of the various centres of mission work. (Applause.) Mr. J. B. ISAAC, who spoke.of the Hall-street Mission, refer- red to a revival that commenced in Buttermarket-streat School several. years ago as the origin of this mission. The mission was now six\ years old. and the workers had toiled on with glalhearts, rejoicing that as the fruit of their lab- ours many were, being edveat* trained, and cultured to take their places in the larger sanctuaries. A Sunday school. had lately been opened, and on the previous day 115-. children were being taught in a room far toe small for their requirements. —Mr. Brough sang "Must-I' go up empty handed P., and Mr. Jowett and Mr. Emraie spoke briefly ef their work' in connection with Hall-street Mission.—Mr. DALE gave,a short sketch of the mission at Silver-street, and spoke of the young people they were. gathering around them and o the thousands who were-untouched by the ' sound of the Gospel in that locality. Much more help was needed, and visitorawers wanted to call upon the people in their homes. The Ragged School in Rewsey-street was a wark lately taken in band with 330 children. The task was a difficult one, ragged and destitute athey were. Still he felt assured•that good impressions were being made, and I moral and-spiritnal lessons were being learned not to be sffaced. (Applause.)—The Coi&inar called upon. Mr. Sinclair,who had been specially engaged in missioa.work at I Mill-lane and Sankey Bridges for two months. His work I had been much, valned. In visiting them doer to door he had bean kindly received, and it was anticipated, that hie. services might be retained in the place. He was recently en- gaged, in a similar capacity in the Manchester City Mission— . Brough sang "Rescue the perishing," anl in a short address referred to the work at Sankey Bridges. They began with cottage services, and had now erected a mission hall in Mill-lane at a cost of £4O: 'That was nowtoo small„ being crowded.—The Rev. JH. JONES rejoiced to see the large gathering present, and said there was a bright future for Warrington Methodism. If ens of Mr. Clapham' k mis- sion chapels could be sesured at a cost of MO, one of the speakers that night had promised to give £20., (Applause.) —Mr. HORROCKS, who has the charge of anew mission in rßattemby-lane, said that although not many weeks old, their mission was rapidly growing. A commodious chapel would very soon be required. They had 160 children's Purees upon the books, with 97 attendances last Sunday. The work was developing in unlikely places. Many were filled with a desire to carry glad tidings to those who would not attend places of worship. He regarded this home missionary zeal as the drreet fruit of the Methodist conven- tion of last year. (Applause.)--A collection was made in aid of the missions in the town, and the Chairman closed the meeting by pronouncing the Benediction.

The fear of further shocks entertained last night have not been realised, but despite the efforts of the authbrities the panic has only partially.. sub- sided. The people are flocking here, as• it is be- lieved to be safer, owing to its high situation and rocky character. LATEST DETAILS.—TERRIBLE LOSS OF LIFE. ROME, THURSDAY, T P.M.—Terrible details are arriving here of the destruction and loss of life caused -by the earthquake shocks yesterday morn- ing. . More than 1,500 people were killed 'in the Genoese Riviera district. ' The . town of Diano Marino no longer exists, and the neighbouring village of Kervo is nearly wholly, destroyed. At Bajardo, a village situated on the top of a hill, the inhabitants sought refuge- in a church, which fell in, killing 300 • people in its ruins. At Oneglia the convict prison is in a very dangerous condition, and the prisoners have had to 'be-- embarked on vesSels in the harbour. The military barracks at Finale Marino have fallen in. S. On Friday afternoon week a general annual meeting ef the Life Governors and Honorary Offieers of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary was held at the Infirmary. Mr W Beamont presided, and there were also present the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs Picirtnere), the Revs R Pileher, 8.A., S. Wilkinson, J Yonze -•i;‘Pr Gomel!, Major Litton Messrs J C Parr, F Monks, T Birchen, J Roberts, T Jolley, J White. R Dobson, Wm Sharpe, J L Tan- stall, and J R Backton (hon treasurer.) ' The folio w- ing' adies were also present—Mrs J White, Mrs Z Armitage, Mrs S Wilkinson, and Mrs T Litton. Let- ters of apology for non-attendance were read from the Rev Father Brown, and Mr T A Withington. HOUSE SURGEON'S REPORT. The House SURGEON (Dr. Richmond) read his annual re- port which stated that during the past year 162 patients were adraittgcl to' the hospital, namely 123 males and 39 females; aaougst these 9 deaths occurred from the follow- ing Causes :—Burns and scalds 3. internal abdominal in- juries 1, enteritis 1, head injuries 1, grave injuries to limbs 3, total 9. The number of patients and of operations presented a striking increase over last year's figures. Indeed, at times daring the year there had been from the gravity of the cases frequent calls on the nursing resources that taxed them to the utmost. The Dis- pensary reported that those out-patients who had been in the course of treatment become home-patients were not en- umerated in the following list of cases treated :—Home patients 606, out-patients 2,137 ; accidents and emergencies 805. Among these 119 deaths had occurred, The past year had been by far the heaviest they had had. This, he sup- posed, was due to the widespread distress during Arhich patients who had hitherto been able to pay their own medical men, had been latterly obliged to come to the hos- pital. At the same time he must say that it bad often seemed as though due inquiry into the circumstances of patients had been neglected by the donors of recommends to the hospital.-0a the motion of the CHAIRMAN, secondtd by Major DITTON, the report was adopted.
